#3580. 10 Perfectly Designed Final Fantasy Magic Cards That Are 10/10, No Notes

A critical hit of Final Fantasy nostalgia

Magic: The Gathering's Final Fantasy crossover set is a love letter to one of gaming's most enduring franchises, bringing together characters, creatures, locations, and iconic moments from across the series' history. With 16 mainline games and even more when counting sequels and spinoffs, Wizards of the Coast had quite the challenge in translating decades of RPG storytelling into a card game with its own language and mechanics.

Packed with hilarious nods, like Suplex, and incredible powerhouses, like Diamond Weapon, it comes as no surprise that Final Fantasy is among the best Universe Beyond sets in the game. But the most perfect designs among them capture a fundamental element of their source material, whether that's Bahamut's devastating Mega Flare, Phoenix Down's clutch resurrection, or the sheer spectacle of summoning Primal Odin.

Whether through clever mechanics or an inspired bit of flavor, these 10 Final Fantasy cards represent the very best of what this crossover has to offer.

Sin anchors the legacy of Final Fantasy antagonists through crushing generational dread, and its card design captures that weight without relying on a lazy stat line. Whenever Sin, Spira's Punishment enters the battlefield or attacks, it exiles a random permanent card from your graveyard, creating a tapped token copy if it's a permanent and repeating the process if a land is hit. Sin is particularly nasty in Commander decks built around graveyard recursion and land synergies, especially when paired with cards like Adrix and Nev, Twincasters, which doubles the tokens it creates, or Hedron Crab, which helps stock the graveyard with fresh targets.

It's an unpredictable engine that turns the remnants of your battlefield into compounding threats throughout the game. Spira’s Punishment also evokes the inescapable cycle of destruction and rebirth that defines Final Fantasy 10, where Spira's people have endured a thousand years of Sin's devastation, rebuilding their lives after each attack and relying on Summoners to temporarily defeat the monster through a ritual sacrifice. Even its seven-mana cost feels entirely appropriate for a monster of its magnitude, though maybe 10 would’ve been more apropos.

Weapons in gaming rarely carry the instant recognition of Cloud Strife's enormous Buster Sword — whether you picture it crudely strapped to his back during the bleak industrial sprawl of early Final Fantasy 7 or dragging it through the mud in Remake — but its significance extends well beyond its imposing silhouette. Passed down through Angeal, Zack, and eventually Cloud, the sword represents the heavy burden of legacy and what one generation leaves behind for another.

Magic: The Gathering captures some of that history through its equipment design, with the Buster Sword giving its wielder a substantial power boost of +3/+2. Whenever said creature hits an opponent directly, you draw a card, then get the opportunity to cast a spell from your hand for free, provided its mana value doesn't exceed the damage dealt. It's a suitably devastating reward for landing a direct hit, and a fitting tribute to one of Final Fantasy's most enduring symbols.

At first glance, Cactuars look like little more than walking houseplants, but when crossed, they can hit you with a devastating flurry of needles. Among Final Fantasy's most recognizable recurring monsters, Cactuars have made a career out of looking harmless before delivering some devastating blows, similar to the goofy-looking Tonberries. MTG’s Jumbo Cactuar follows that lineage beautifully through a seven-mana creature with a relatively unassuming 1/7 stat line. It looks like any regular green common creature, until you notice its ability, 10,000 Needles, which gives it a whopping +9,999/+0 whenever it attacks.

That's right, this seemingly harmless plant suddenly becomes a 10,000-power monster capable of flattening just about anything in its path. It's an almost comically literal interpretation of the Cactuar family's signature attack, and that's what makes it so brilliant (and hilarious). There's no need for elaborate transformations or complicated synergies. Magic simply takes one of Final Fantasy's most recognizable monster abilities and turns it into a devastating combat trick.

While Final Fantasy 13 remains one of the most divisive entries in the franchise’s storied history, Lightning herself stands tall as one of its absolute finest protagonists. She’s a relentless soldier defined by unwavering resolve and immediate action, a former Guardian Corps sergeant who goes AWOL during the violent exile of Bodhum's citizens, derailing a Purge train and battling through the Hanging Edge to rescue her sister.

Her Magic card captures that uncompromising spirit right out of the gate. A three-mana creature with first strike, trample, and lifelink is already a formidable combatant, but her stagger ability is what makes the design sing. Whenever Lightning, Army of One deals combat damage to an opponent, all damage dealt to that player and their permanents by any source is doubled until your next turn. It’s a brilliant adaptation of FF13’s defining combat rhythm, where staggering an enemy leaves them completely exposed to devastating follow-up attacks. Magic turns her into the tip of the spear for an all-out assault, translating one of the series' signature mechanics into a game-winning tactical engine.

Zack Fair's story is one of Final Fantasy 7’s most heartbreaking, particularly because his final moments have such a profound impact on Cloud's journey. Magic honors the character with a 0/1 legendary creature that enters with a +1/+1 counter on it. You can play one mana to sacrifice Zack Fair and give another creature indestructible, Zack’s counters, and even the equipment attached to him.

It's a thoughtful piece of design that essentially turns his death into an act of protection and inheritance. There's no elaborate transformation or complicated combination of abilities, Zack's final act becomes a playable mechanic, allowing another hero to carry his strength and equipment forward. It’s hard to imagine a more poignant tribute to a character whose entire legacy is defined by passing the torch, and some players have found clever ways to abuse it by looping him from the graveyard with reanimation engines like Sun Titan or Lurrus, repeatedly granting their board indestructible while constantly passing his stat boosts down the line.

Aerith’s power has always stemmed from gentle resilience rather than overwhelming force. She’s a healer, after all, and the last surviving Cetra, hiding in plain sight selling flowers in the Sector 5 slums while carrying the solitary burden of the Planet's survival. In Magic, Aerith Gainsborough is a 2/2 legendary creature that enters the battlefield with lifelink, and whenever you gain life, she receives a +1/+1 counter. This makes her progressively stronger as she supports your other creatures and keeps your life total at a healthy advantage over your opponents.

However, the real stroke of genius comes when Aerith dies. Every legendary creature you control receives +1/+1 counters equal to the number Aerith had accumulated during her time on the battlefield. It's a beautiful mechanical interpretation of her legacy, particularly considering the profound impact her death has on Cloud and the rest of the party in the original game. Aerith's influence doesn't disappear when she's gone, but lives on through the people she leaves behind. And it’s even better when you’ve already got a 12/12 Eldrazi on the board.

Final Fantasy 10’s Yuna is a summoner first and foremost, making her one of the most natural candidates for a Magic card built around enchantments and their associated creatures. What makes Yuna, Hope of Spira particularly clever is how the card encourages players to assemble a collection of saga creatures, the special enchantments introduced in the Final Fantasy set to represent the franchise's iconic summons.

During your turn, Yuna grants herself and your other enchantment creatures trample, lifelink, and ward 2, making the entire group considerably more difficult to deal with. She can also return an enchantment from your graveyard to the battlefield at the end of your turn, but with a finality counter on it that prevents it from returning to the graveyard again. It's a fantastic representation of Yuna's role as a summoner, turning her into the centerpiece of an entire Aeon-focused strategy with enchantment creatures cards like Yojimbo, Bahamut, Knights of Round, and more.

Speaking of Knights of Round, it's as much a powerful Magic card as it is a legendary summon in the games. First appearing as the ultimate secret Materia in Final Fantasy 7, tucked away on the unmapped Round Island and requiring a Gold Chocobo just to reach, it calls forth 13 holy knights to rain down an unskippable two-minute-long assault of apocalyptic damage. It was the absolute pinnacle of endgame excess, forcing players to sit back and watch a cinematic spectacle unfold while Sephiroth’s health bar disintegrated.

Magic’s interpretation of it is every bit as theatrical. Designed as an eight-mana Saga creature, Knights of Round gradually builds an army by creating three 2/2 Knight tokens across each of its first four chapters. That’s twelve knights in total, before its fifth and final chapter delivers Ultimate End, buffing your entire board with +2/+2 and dropping an indestructible counter onto each of your creatures. It's a wonderfully patient piece of design that rewards players for waiting out the full summon sequence, turning that notoriously long animation into a looming, game-ending countdown your opponents can only watch in dread. Unless they’re in blue, of course.

Sephiroth’s transformation from celebrated First Class SOLDIER hero to the cold One-Winged Angel remains one of gaming’s most devastating character arcs. He wasn't just a villain; he was Shinra's ultimate hero whose sanity shattered the moment he uncovered his horrific origins inside the Nibelheim mansion: he was engineered from the alien calamity Jenova. He burned Nibelheim to the ground and began viewing humanity as mere parasites. His tragic fall shifted the entire scope of Final Fantasy 7 from an anti-corporate resistance story into an apocalyptic cosmic horror.

Magic imbues that journey onto a double-faced creature that grows more dangerous as the battlefield descends into chaos. On his front side, Sephiroth, Fabled SOLDIER allows you to sacrifice another creature whenever he enters or attacks, drawing a card in return. Meanwhile, whenever another creature dies, you drain one life from an opponent and gain one yourself. Once that second ability has resolved for the fourth time in a single turn, Sephiroth transforms into his One-Winged Angel form, granting an emblem that keeps the life-drain engine running permanently whenever creatures die. You can also even stack that with his second ability, letting you sac as many creatures as you like in exchange for that many card draws. It's an inspired way to represent Sephiroth's growing power, turning the battlefield into a ticking clock as his enemies fall around him.

Final Fantasy 11 has no shortage of formidable enemies, but few developed the same legendary reputation as Absolute Virtue. This optional superboss became infamous for its extraordinary durability and punishing difficulty, earning a reputation as one of the most frustrating encounters in the entire franchise. Absolute Virtue could repeatedly unleash powerful abilities borrowed from multiple player classes, including Benediction, which allowed it to restore enormous amounts of health just when victory seemed within reach. Its substantial passive regeneration made matters even worse, turning the encounter into an exhausting war of attrition that demanded meticulous coordination from an entire alliance of players. Some groups spent more than 18 hours attempting to defeat it, cementing its place in MMO history as one of gaming's most notorious boss encounters.

Magic distills its intimidating presence through an eight-mana 8/8 construction that can't be countered when it’s played, plus it has flying, of course. Even more terrifying is its secondary ability, which grants you protection from each of your opponents, effectively making you untouchable while Absolute Virtue remains on the battlefield. Opponents can’t attack you, target you with spells, or even enchant you. It's a fitting translation of a boss that once seemed practically impossible to defeat, forcing opponents to find a way around its defenses before they can even think about bringing it down.

#3579. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3578. Inside PS, The Private Members-Only Terminals at LAX, Miami, and Paris Airports

There are 10 terminals at the Los Angeles International Airport. One through nine are for the general public: terminal one for Southwest, terminal two for Virgin Atlantic, the international hub in the numberless terminal B. Each one is packed with weary, edgy travelers lined up for security, coffee, or a meal. You arrive at your terminal via rideshare and depart via rideshare—so long as your ride is a premium black car. If it isn’t, you must take a 20-minute bus ride to a parking lot called “LAX-it,” where you wait amongst the hordes for your UberX to arrive as it slowly inches through crippling traffic.

The 10th terminal promises to deliver you from this misery. It’s around the back of the airport complex, off the 105 in El Segundo, next to several cargo holds and a Gate Gourmet facility where airplane meals are carted off to various jets on the tarmac. When you arrive, no one asks for a boarding pass. A security guard checks your name off a list, and a valet whisks away your bags with care before you’re ushered into your own private suite with amenities galore: squishy velvet couches and boucle chairs, Assouline coffee table books, free iPhone chargers, and chocolate-covered almonds and gummy bears. A fridge comes with sparkling waters and canned matcha drinks—a far cry from the plastic Dasani bottles found at Hudson News. A private bathroom boasts Le Labo soaps.

While you’re waiting for your flight, you can get a manicure, a table massage, or even a haircut. You can request a pair of Normatec Elite compression boots (retail price: $1,099) to help with your circulation before takeoff. Or if you are feeling more social, you can head to “the Salon,” where abstract art hangs on the wall and chandeliers dangle from the ceiling. Order the coconut chia pudding or bagel-and-lox platter if you’re there for breakfast, duck confit agnolotti or a Mediterranean chicken panini on house-made ciabatta for lunch. For dinner, there’s a New York strip, and caviar service is always available.

When it’s time to go, you’ll pass through a private security check with a dedicated TSA agent. Then you’ll climb in a BMW (suitcases already loaded) which drives you across the tarmac directly to your plane. Forget boarding with Zone 8 or gatechecking your carry-on.

The Salon at PS at LAX, designed by Elle Decor A-List interior designer Cliff Fong.

This is PS at LAX—a private, members only terminal at Los Angeles International. It’ll cost you to get in: One-time access to the Salon (and nothing else) without a membership is priced at $1,295. For frequent fliers, an annual baseline membership starts at $1,250 and goes up to $4,850. Private suites cost an additional $3,650 or $4,950 for four people, depending on the type of membership.

Unsurprisingly, it’s become a see-and-don’t-be-seen hub for LA celebrities wary of attracting the camera-wielding masses at commercial airports (and the paparazzi that stake out the terminal). Gigi Hadid, Gabrielle Union, Hailey Bieber, Jamie Foxx, and Kourtney Kardashian are just some of the famous faces that are known to frequent PS at LAX.

But this year, PS is pushing beyond the Hollywood stars eager to escape the clutches of Deuxmoi. In the past six months, the firm has opened private terminals in Miami (taking over the historic Pan-Am space) and Dallas. Paris is coming in early 2027. The seclusion, the gourmet food, and the luxurious interiors (curated by Elle Decor A-List designers Jean Liu for Dallas and Cliff Fong for Miami and LA) are all nice draws, but there's another reason PS CEO Amina Belouizdad Porter cites for why customers are willing to shell out thousands of dollars on top of a first-class ticket.

The Atlanta airport on March 23, 2026. Government shutdowns have caused disastrous scenes at American commercial terminals.

Because, well, it has been. The last fiscal year has seen three government shutdowns, the longest of which lasted for 76 days. TSA Deputy Administrator Ha Nguyen McNeill told Congress that the agency experienced the longest security wait times in its 24-year history during the shutdown that stretched from February 14 to April 30, 2026. Some airports, including Atlanta, had lines up to five hours long. The logistical meltdowns hit at a time when air travel has never been more popular: In 2025, nearly 907 million people flew commercially in the United States. Belouizdad Porter says that those disruptions led to a direct increase in PS customers.

The growing crowds at airport lounges also nudged some travelers over the edge. Credit card companies long ago realized that offering lounge access enticed new customers, with Chase, American Express, Citi, Capital One, and more getting in the game. But demand exceeded square footage, and many of those lounges suffered from overcrowding and subpar service, selling the dream of an aero oasis that never was.

“There have never been more airport lounges,” David Mack writes in the New York Times, “Yet there also have never seemed to be more lounges that are not worth the hassle…Sometimes the lines for the lounges are the longest in the airport.”

(Though the only thing worse than an overcrowded airport lounge might be getting stranded outside. Reddit is currently up in arms about the obscene food prices at the newly renovated Burbank Airport in California—price tag: $1.3 billion—where a cheese and bean burrito costs $25.)

Another contributing factor? The rising costs of private jets. While the terms “one percent” or “.1 percent” are often thrown around when it comes to PJ owners, the reality is only 0.003 percent of America’s population can afford even fractional ownership. Demand for private aircraft surged after the pandemic, raising prices, and now the average net worth of those who own a jet is $190 million. For those with fractional ownership, it’s $140 million. Yet there are still plenty of mere decamillionaires looking to dodge the misery of the airport. As Sartre put it: Hell is other people.

Previously, “You could either fly round-trip first class for $6,000 but deal with the airport, the friction, and the crowd,” Belouizdad Porter says. “Or you could fly private round-trip and it's $200,000.” PS operates somewhere in between. “I think there’s a real appetite for that middle ground: the convenience of private aviation without the commitment or expense of chartering an entire plane,” says Lucie Kittel, founder of luxury travel advisory firm Domino Travel.

And besides, even if you do reach the level of private jet ownership, you still can’t always avoid the flying masses. A midsize jet that fits six to nine people costs between $10 and $20 million dollars and can fly 2,000 to 3,000 nautical miles. If it’s on the shorter end of that range, it can just make a trip from New York to California—but not to Europe. There’s also the issue of safety: The country is currently facing a pilot shortage, and more experienced candidates often work with mainstream airlines who can provide higher salaries. Larger planes can also better navigate rough weather.

Carriers like United and Delta know all of this, which is why they’re beefing up their luxury experiences. Delta recently announced it was investing over $1 billion in retrofitting its premium cabins, and new Delta One Terminals at JFK and LAX allow first-class ticket holders to avoid overcrowded TSA lines and the standard lounge. “Most of my clients flying out of JFK are choosing Delta One,” Kittel adds, “and they love the experience.”

Thanks to the artificial intelligence boom—the latest phase of a 15-year bull market for stocks—there’s been an explosion of multi-multi-millionaires in America. While not all of them can fly private, they certainly can devote large sums of money to separating themselves from the hoi polloi. Both startups like PS and established players are now competing for that sub-ultra-wealthy dollar.

#3577. Susie Wiles Is Out. What Will Trump Do When He Runs Out of Women to Fire?

You know how after millions of people make clear that they despise not just your political project but also you personally, the logical response is to triple down on the specific things they hate?

That’s Donald Trump’s signature move. Three days after Democrats flipped seven Senate seats—nine if you feel bullish on Mississippi and Alaska—and secured a House majority, winning 253 seats and counting, the president announced that his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, would be replaced by Stephen Miller.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Even though polls indicating a blue wave proliferated before the election, this particular outcome still comes as a surprise. After all, Wiles had apparently proven her ability to ride out storms before—including everything that rocked Trump’s 2024 campaign, which Wiles managed, and her choice to sit for 10 interviews with Vanity Fair’s Chris Whipple in 2025, during which she discussed Elon Musk’s drug use and JD Vance’s true motives for embracing Trump. “Despite his travails, Trump needs Wiles and almost everyone around him knows it,” Whipple recently wrote in a follow-up story tracing rumors of Wiles’s imminent axing.

But now Wiles’s luck has finally run out. Why? Perhaps because she is, in the end, a woman.

Trump’s first term was marked by all sorts of chaos, including frequent arrivals to and departures from the White House. (Remember Omarosa?) But it doesn’t take Jessica Fletcher to detect that this time around, there’s a distinct pattern when it comes to whom Trump is willing to toss aside when the going gets rough. The scalps of the no-scalps era all have barrel curls. As Texas representative Jasmine Crockett observed in April, “He will throw the incompetent women under the bus a lot faster than the incompetent men.”

On March 5, following an uprising against the administration’s mass-deportation effort that culminated in two protesters being killed by ICE agents in Minnesota, Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem was axed. After wrath over the administration’s botched handling of the Epstein files, Attorney General Pam Bondi was fired in April.

Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Trump’s labor secretary, resigned later that month amid a misconduct investigation. Tulsi Gabbard, the director of national intelligence, who couldn’t sell Trump’s disastrous war with Iran, submitted her resignation in May, after her husband was diagnosed with cancer. Press secretary Karoline Leavitt stepped down—of her own accord—in August. Following an embarrassing Wall Street Journal investigation, Kimberly Guilfoyle, the ambassador to Greece—and former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr.—was forced to resign last month.

Though you may have already forgotten all about her, Katie Zacharia had perhaps the least distinguished tenure of all: She gave her first briefing as Trump’s new press secretary on a Tuesday and was forced out by Friday of the same week. Shortly before Wiles’s ouster this week, Harmeet Dhillon, who helped kill DEI after joining the civil rights division of Trump’s Justice Department, announced she was stepping down.

All this, and Pete Hegseth still has a job.

What are we to make of the fact that Trump’s departed all happen to harbor two X chromosomes? Could it be, perhaps, that President “Grab ’Em by the Pussy” has a problem with women—even the loyalists who are largely responsible for helping him claw his way back into the White House in the first place? (Does Trump win, or even run, in 2024 without Wiles? It’s a possibility I’d like to see Rodham author Curtis Sittenfeld explore in an upcoming novel.)

The one thing we can be sure about is that, as of right now, there are only three women left in Trump’s 21-person Cabinet. The members of that trio—Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Education Secretary Linda McMahon, and Kelly Loeffler, administrator of the Small Business Administration—might want to watch their blowout. (So should Natalie Harp.) Perhaps after they go, Trump will start employing the principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion while stabbing his allies in the back.

#3576. One of the Best QLED TVs of 2026 Is Over $1,300 Off Right Now

TCL has been pushing the boundaries of QLED TVs, making some of the best in the market at very competitive prices. This year, the company released its QM8L model, introducing a new design and impressive features and specs to a series that isn't even their flagship. Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $1,197.99 (originally $2,499.99), $100 cheaper than it was just earlier this month, reaching its lowest price since it launched in April, according to price-tracking tools. Larger sizes are also seeing substantial discounts.

One of the first things you'll notice about the QM8L is the “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets, which is a huge advantage QLEDs have over OLEDs. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits—seeing as the brightest OLED TV on the market only reaches 700 nits, no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming (thanks in part to TCL's "Halo Control"), and incredible contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

As many of us won't manually calibrate our TVs, the picture modes you can switch to in the settings will be most people's go-to. This TV's "Filmmaker mode" provides accurate color and picture, and if you're a gamer, you can use the native 144Hz high-refresh rate. If you don't already have a surround sound system at home and want to keep a minimalist setup, the QM8L comes with Dolby Atmos-ready Bang & Olufsen speakers, which offer above-average audio output compared to most TVs. You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.

By now, basketball fans are surely aware that Ernie Johnson is leaving Inside the NBA after the 2026-2027 NBA season. Johnson made the announcement at the end of October, and fans and celebrities alike have since been honoring him. One of the most emotional tributes, though, came from Johnson’s longtime co-hosts, Charles Barkley, who spoke about the news during an episode of the talk show. I was already in my feelings over the on-air tribute but, now, that’s amped up a bit since I’ve heard Johnson’s first-hand account.

Johnson initially revealed his news in a social media video that eventually went viral on October 28, and he spoke about it again at the top of Inside’s broadcast that evening. Following that opening, Johnson teed up the show, as per usual, by introducing co-hosts Barkley, Kenny Smith and Shaquille O’Neal. When Johnson threw it to Barkley, however, he was misty-eyed and momentarily at a loss for words. Johnson admitted on The Dan LeBatard Show (as seen on YouTube) that he was surprised, saying:

I was concerned, at first, because the camera was on him and he wasn't saying anything, and he had to kind of — like he was struggling and I was like, 'Oh, what's going on here?' The moments don't get much better than that for me when I think about the last few days. Because look, I've said it before, you guys have heard me, we love each other. We've been together for so long. We would do anything for one another.

That night, when the camera was on him, the usually humorous Barkley took a few seconds to compose himself. He eventually recovered, simply saying, “That was tough,” in a low and solemn voice. “Sir Charles” then proceeded to give a truly warm tribute to Johnson, which beautifully summed up the 26 years they’ve worked together. Check out Barkley’s tribute, and those of Smith and O’Neal by watching the video below:

Months ago, Charles Barkley claimed he would retire after this season and, in the process of doing so, he let slip that Johnson was doing the same. Barkley voiced his desire for both him and his co-host to step away from the show together. Johnson didn’t immediately confirm his plans for weeks, leaving much uncertainty. In the video, Johnson explained that he wanted to step away from the show as a way of slowing down a bit in order to spend some time with his family and focus on other ventures. Johnson also said this of his on-air tribute:

It was emotional for me. I mean, I was holding it together all day long and it was like, ‘Oh, man. I'm watching Chuck struggle with this.’ But that just speaks to the relationship we all have.

Charles Barkley Shares More Thoughts On Retiring From Inside The NBA, And I’m Starting To Believe He’ll Do It This Time

Johnson began hosting Inside back in the fall of 1990 and, under his leadership, the show became a must-watch program for basketball devotees like myself. The “Godfather” has been present for the series’ biggest moments, including its move from TNT to ESPN last season. Considering the veteran broadcaster’s long tenure with the program, the notion of him no longer hosting is somewhat hard to think about. What’s more is that there’s still the question of whether Barkley will truly retire (this time) as he declared.

Whatever the case, ESPN is reportedly committed to Inside the NBA regardless of Ernie Johnson and Charles Barkley’s plans. I’m not sure I’m ready to think about the prospect of the show being with two of its key members. For now, though, I’m just relishing this final season with the core four and hoping it produces even more memorable moments like Barkley’s sentimental tribute.

#3574. How the ‘Glee’ and ‘Girls’ Revivals Can Avoid Mistakes Made by Other TV Reboots

The blue-tinged afterglow of the 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both the House and Senate, unleashed a burst of online millennial optimism. Some have credited a pair of newly revived Obama-era coming of age TV shows that often got political themselves, Ryan Murphy’s Glee and Lena Dunham’s Girls, with being a precursor to the Blue Wave.

But for all of the internet’s excitement for new episodes of Glee and Girls , no one said aging beloved characters (who is Hannah Horvath at 40?), or addressing the current sociopolitical moment (will Sue Sylvester in a MAGA hat be inevitable?!) would come without risk. How do the Girls and Glee reboots meet nostalgic expectations while delivering something new and prescient about where the world is now? Perhaps Dunham and Murphy can draw lessons about aging gracefully in adaptation from revivals that have aired before them.

Ahead, a guide to do’s and don’ts for the return of generational TV, from the second coming of Sex and the City to Roseanne’s rocky renewal.

Riding a high from his Emmy-nominated shows including Ted Lasso and Shrinking (Apple TV), plus Rooster (HBO), series creator Bill Lawrence relaunched Scrubs, now airing its second season on ABC, into a post-Abbott Elementary landscape—where network TV craves workplace comedies for its airwaves. It seems that the folks behind Glee and Girls, respectively, have found the right moment to return to TV. Murphy has spoken about Glee’s recent streaming resurgence for younger audiences, and Dunham is coming off a headline-making book tour for her bestselling memoir Famesick, written about her time making Girls 1.0.

Rather than write themselves out of the show’s controversial final season, in which most of the show’s central cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, Sarah Chalke, were sidelined in favor of an entirely new group of characters, the creative team opted to retcon the entire ninth season and start fresh for the reboot. That means Glee can freely pretend its own flashforward—in which Rachel Berry is a surrogate mother for fellow Glee Club pals Kurt and Blaine could be abandoned. And maybe Shoshanna never decided she was too good for the rest of the Girls and they can all be dysfunctional friends again…right?

A political sketch titled “Oh Honey,” which reunited original cast members Debra Messing, Eric McCormack, Sean Hayes, and Megan Mullally in support of Hillary Clinton ahead of the 2016 presidential election, may not have prevented a Donald Trump presidency. But it did garner millions of views online, earning the attention of top NBC brass who hoped to capitalize on the nostalgia by relaunching Will & Grace in 2017. While the Glee Club has yet to release their own teaser, Dunham announced the Girls revival via four-way video call with cast members Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, and Zosia Mamet that promptly sent the internet into a tailspin.

While the Will & Grace revival lasted for three seasons largely because of its ability to engage with the day’s political issues, particularly as they related to the LGBTQ+ community, some felt the show became too steeped in Trumpland. In one episode, a Trump-supporting Karen even gets staunchly liberal Grace a job decorating his Oval Office. Girls and Glee will have to strike a similarly delicate balance with their own returns—incorporating the current political landscape in ways that feel natural to the narrative, as much as one can when often tone-deaf show choir kids and Brooklyn hipsters are involved.

Just as And Just Like That made a splash by murdering Mr. Big in the first episode via Peloton-induced heart attack, Glee and Girls should aim for maximum impact upon arrival. Maybe Adam Driver’s character meets his end while going method for a role and learning a dangerous new skill. As for Glee, perhaps the character played by Grammy-winning Finneas O’Connell (brother and music producer of Billie Eilish), could go up in a blaze of glory. Despite getting his start with a four-episode arc in the show’s final season, in 2020 O’Connell claimed that he’d never seen Glee, including the episodes he was in.

Taking a show outside of its comfort zone in the right ways raises the stakes—and highlights core tensions from the original series (see also: Miranda shown riding the subway for the first time). But some viewers felt And Just Like That… showrunner Michael Patrick King’s inclusion of diverse voices into the narrative veered too far outside of the shoebox with Che Diaz, the divisive podcast-cohost–slash-comedian–slash–veterinarian-office-worker that took the brunt of audience ire over freshly sober Miranda’s decision to divorce her husband Steve. New characters can become de facto villains for a series revival, particularly if they interfere with cherished dynamics from the show’s first run.

The return of Kelsey Grammer’s sitcom hero Frasier Crane was undercut by the absence of breakout supporting characters Niles and Daphne, as actors David Hyde Pierce and Jane Leeves did not reprise their roles for the reboot. Luckily, the core four of Girls have already signed on for their five-episode revival, and several Glee alums are in talks for its reboot, including series lead Lea Michele.

In addition to some of the creative challenges facing Frasier 2.0, the former NBC sitcom was welcomed back on Paramount+, a lesser-known streaming platform in comparison to Netflix or Peacock. At least it wasn’t Helen Hunt and Paul Reiser’s Mad About You, another ’90s NBC comedy that got its grand return on…Spectrum (?!) in 2019. Girls will air on HBO’s streaming partner, Max, and Glee is in the works via Disney+ and Hulu—barring any major industry mergers.

The Roseanne reboot earned new resonance in the zeitgeist—and major ratings on ABC—for its authentic depiction of a working-class Middle America family under Trump’s first presidency. Like the original 1988 series, the revival focused on the economic and social realities of surviving as a lower-income family in America. And like Will & Grace before it, Roseanne organically, even comically, depicted familial political divides by portraying Roseanne Conner as a Trump voter and her sister Jackie as a Hillary Clinton supporter.

After series lead Roseanne Barr tweeted a racist slur about Valerie Jarrett, a senior aide to President Barack Obama, ABC Entertainment president Channing Dungey terminated the series on May 29, 2018, following its renewal for an 11th season on the network. Then, the following month, ABC announced it was ordering 10 episodes of a spin-off about the family titled The Conners, which regenerated by killing off the character of Roseanne, ending just last year after seven seasons on the air. If anything, the show’s unlikely staying power proves that if a show sticks to its DNA, it can outlast even the messiest of scandals.

The four-episode return of Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel’s mother-daughter dramedy was rightfully docked for its extended, gratuitous Stars Hollow musical involving Tony Award-winning performers (and ex-spouses) Sutton Foster and Christian Borle. But a bit of superfluous song-and-dance naturally feels right at home for Glee, and even Girls—an encore version of Marnie singing Kanye West’s “Stronger” would reach cringeworthy new depths.

The pregnancy revelation that ends Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life should have kicked the revival off, not concluded its story. Instead, A Year in the Life emphasizes just how little Rory and Lorelei have grown in the years since Gilmore Girls ended, only to leave the revival’s most compelling leap forward for its final moments—and totally unresolved. After a decade, the bait-and-switch still burns, which speaks to the divisive, and enduring, nature of TV returns themselves. As for the next chapters of Glee and Girls, may the writers’ rooms hear our post-election pleas.

#3573. Sydney Sweeney’s Extremely R-Rated 131-Minute Thriller Is Officially Streaming on HBO

Perfect for those who love an outrageous twist

Despite its overwhelming commercial success, Freida McFadden’s psychological thriller, The Housemaid, is far from a perfect read. Trope-heavy and full of obvious contrivances, The Housemaid sets up a tense domestic thriller premise that is meant to be consumed as a fast-paced popcorn novel. This, however, sets the stage for a pulpy screen adaptation, one that mimics the conventions of a lurid thriller with some decent character writing to round things out.

Bridesmaids director Paul Feig’s The Housemaid lives up to these expectations. Formulaic but utterly entertaining, the film features Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried as characters that seem to be pitted against each other. The Housemaid is a great fit for anyone who likes erotic thrillers of the Verity variety, wherein the plot features some sort of unexpected twist to keep things interesting. If you’ve been meaning to watch The Housemaid from the comfort of your home, the film is available to stream on HBO Max right now.

Recently paroled Millie (Sweeney) tries to put her past behind her by working as a live-in maid for Nina (Seyfried), who lives with her husband, Andrew (Brandon Sklenar), and daughter, Cece (Indiana Elle). Nina needs help because she is pregnant, and Millie needs to maintain a lawful employment status, making the arrangement feasible at first. Nina’s suburban mansion in Great Neck, Long Island, is opulent to the point of appearing gaudy, giving Millie all the more reason to commit to the job seriously.

Unfortunately, things start to feel off after some time. Millie is asked to stay in an attic bedroom that locks from the outside, and Nina starts making veiled threats, asking Millie to stay away from her husband. Things escalate quickly, going from mild accusations to full-blown breakdowns that make Millie feel horribly trapped inside a ridiculously spacious mansion.

The Housemaid toys with our expectations as it builds its suspense, allowing us to immerse ourselves in the minute details of Nina and Millie’s frayed dynamic. Is Nina truly troubled like everyone wants us to believe, or is there a grander conspiracy at play here? Although Nina’s erratic behavior is a cause for genuine concern, Millie and Andrew are drawn closer amid this chaos, leading to the start of a complicated relationship that might change everything we know about these characters.

Unlike the source material, The Housemaid takes itself a bit too seriously. That, however, doesn’t get in the way of the curveballs that Feig throws at us after the shocking midway twist is revealed. Most pulpy thrillers thrive on this formula, including The Voyeurs, which is yet another engaging movies starring Sweeney. The Housemaid makes good use of this tonal shift, allowing characters like Nina to unravel more layers of her complex, inconsistent behavior.

Even before the film hones in on the truth, The Housemaid is smart enough to keep us guessing. Nina’s behavior (which often encroaches on horror movie territory) is backed up by whispers from her high-society friends and anecdotes from other house staff. Andrew’s perspective is also crucial here. He comes across as a doting husband and father, heartbroken that his wife is no longer the person he fell in love with. Millie’s escalating attraction to Andrew fuels these confusing rumors, but we’re often given glimpses of a truth we’re not yet privy to.

What The Housemaid does accomplish is a sense of dramatic climax that is significantly toned down in the book. “There’s things that work in the book that are really satisfying, but on the big screen you always want more," Feig told The Hollywood Reporter to explain his need to up the ante. Feig also uses perspective shifts to tie disparate clues together, and Seyfried’s standout performance contains subtle hints for eagle-eyed audiences to decipher. Things turn sleazy when they need to, without diving into the pure camp of genre entries like Body Double (1984) or Wild Things (1998).

If you like entertaining psychological thrillers with a pulpy edge, The Housemaid is a solid choice. This is no Gone Girl, but taut atmosphere and pacing make this movie feel more than serviceable.

#3572. These Sony ANC Headphones Are on Sale for $128 Right Now

It's hard to convince yourself to spend nearly half a grand on premium headphones, like the Sony WH-1000XM6, even if you consider yourself an audiophile. Not everyone can afford those prices, which is why the budget, mid-tier, and premium tiers exist. While the premium 1000XM6 headphones are over three times the price of the mid-tier Sony WH-CH730N, they're not three times as good. The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179) right now, the lowest price they've ever been according to price-tracking tools, and they offer an amazing value for your money.

It's pretty impressive what $128 in headphones gets you in 2026. The CH730N uses the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0. The Adaptive Sound Control feature can detect your activity (walking, sitting down, loud environment, etc.) and automatically switch the level of ANC and transparency to make your experience as comfortable and seamless as possible.

The microphones are decent and use a feature to isolate your voice in noisy environments. I love that there's an AUX connection to give you the option, which seems to be coming back with newer headphones. The design is light and will feel like plastic, but they are comfortable to wear for long sessions. If you're looking to maximize the quality of headphones you can get for your money, the Sony WH-CH730N offer a pretty compelling option at $128.

As soon as the news came out that there would be a movie about the making of Rocky, I was pumped! The timing truly is perfect, as this great sports film is celebrating its 50th anniversary this year. So, Rocky fans are sure to raise their fists in the air as they head to theaters. However, Ryan Gosling has already done that. Yes, that's right, Ryan Gosling gave I Play Rocky his stamp of approval, which is making me put this movie high on my watchlist.

Early reviews of I Play Rocky were great. With its star, Anthony Ippolito, nailing Sylvester Stallone’s voice and swagger, I felt like it would be easy to love this upcoming flick. However, it just got easier, because while AnnaSophia Robb (who plays Sylvester Stallone's wife, Sasha) was on The Today Show, she spoke about none other than Ryan Gosling giving the cast his stamp of approval:

It was wild. I have never experienced anything like that. We’re at CinemaCon and we’re doing, you know, press. It’s absolute chaos. And all of a sudden, there’s this kerfuffle and I turn around and Ryan Gosling is there. And he goes, ‘Is this the I Play Rocky cast? I love the movie! It was terrific!’

Wow! Given what a talented actor Ryan Gosling is, it has to be such an honor to receive a compliment from him. Just as I was already excited for the drama, The Notebook actor hyped me up even more.

I would assume that no matter how accomplished or famous you are, to have someone you look up to compliment your work must mean the world. That was certainly the case for the cast of I Play Rocky during this interaction with the Project Hail Mary star, as Robb continued:

And I was gobsmacked. My jaw was on the floor and it was just, it meant so much because I had just watched him in Project Hail Mary and I loved it. And just to have somebody you’ve been watching your whole life love the film. It just, it meant the world. And we’re all sitting there like, wow.

Yes, it’s very easy to be a Ryan Gosling fan when you watch his best romances and top underrated movies. So, I can only imagine how overwhelming it must have been to be on the receiving end of his compliment. It’s clear the La La Land actor knows a good movie when he sees it and isn’t afraid to give acclaim to it. (Plus it doesn't hurt that his latest movie, Project Hail Mary, features some very notable Rocky references.)

As I Play Rocky makes its way to theaters, I'm happy we now know that Ryan Gosling gave it his stamp of approval. I’m sure he won’t be the only one once we all get to see talented actors shape the story of how the masterpiece of Rocky was made. You all have the chance to feel what Gosling is feeling as the 2026 movie release is playing in select theaters now.

#3570. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle Are Moving Again

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have reportedly found a new home in the Cotswolds, less than three months after their return to the United Kingdom. But anyone who thinks they’ve bought a new home will be disappointed. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who had been staying at the residence of a wealthy entrepreneur friend since August 26, have reportedly left the main house on the property to move into another residence located within the same estate, according to Daily Mail journalist Richard Eden. “They were living in the main house,” a person close to the entrepreneur told the British newspaper. “They have now moved to a property on the estate.” The move reportedly took place before Harry and Meghan left for a vacation abroad with their children.

Since the couple returned to the United Kingdom, their search for a new home in Britain has been a hotly debated topic, especially in light of their disagreements with the royal family and security concerns. The mystery surrounding their residence has fueled speculation and various theories. Where would the Sussexes choose to settle? That was the question echoing everywhere on social media and in the press. For security reasons, the details of their living arrangements have always remained confidential.

As reported by the British media, the couple and their two children had been staying at a property owned by a wealthy friend, nestled in the Cotswolds countryside—an area Harry and Meghan already knew well. In 2018, the year of their wedding, they rented a prestigious farmhouse in the region for two years—a historic property with an estimated value of 4.12 million British pounds (about $5.5 million), part of the Great Tew Estate. The residence included a four-bedroom farmhouse, a barn converted into living quarters, and a separate cottage with two additional bedrooms. The property also featured extensive grounds and a heated patio. Over the years, the Cotswolds, in the English countryside, have become a retreat for numerous celebrities, including Jeremy Clarkson, David and Victoria Beckham, and Kate Moss. A few weeks ago the Duchess of Sussex was photographed at The Three Horseshoes, a quaint pub near Burford, in the company of Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi. In 2024, DeGeneres and de Rossi left the United States to move to the Cotswolds, where they live on a large estate surrounded by greenery.

The Sussexes’ housing history in the United Kingdom, however, has been quite eventful. Before leaving the United Kingdom, the couple lived at Frogmore Cottage in Windsor, a property made available to Harry and Meghan by Queen Elizabeth II. In 2023, however, the two royals left the residence. The decision came a few months after the publication of the duke’s memoir, Spare. To renovate Frogmore Cottage, approximately 2.4 million British pounds (about $3.2 million) went into transforming two existing buildings into a single-family home. The renovations were extensive: The ceiling beams and floor structures were replaced, the electrical system was redone, new gas and water lines were installed, and a soundproofing system costing approximately 50,000 British pounds (about $67,000) was reportedly put in place. Despite the significant spend, the Sussexes left the property for good after moving overseas.

Even before settling in Windsor, Harry and Meghan lived at Nottingham Cottage, within the Kensington Palace complex. It was a rather small residence that apparently hadn’t won Meghan over. In the Netflix documentary Harry & Meghan, the duchess recalled with a touch of irony that the name Kensington Palace suggested something grand, while the reality was quite different: “Kensington Palace sounds very regal, of course it does. It says ‘palace’ in the name. But Nottingham Cottage was so small!” Harry added that the house had very low ceilings and was even slightly slanted.

The new home in the Cotswolds could therefore be a practical solution for the Sussexes, at least until they figure out their plans in the United Kingdom. Meghan’s professional commitments may also take her away from England again. The duchess is expected to move temporarily to Australia next year to participate in the filming of Junior MasterChef, the cooking show she is set to cohost. Prince Harry and their two children might join her during her stay in Australia, but there’s no confirmation of that yet.

The identity of the estate’s current owner remains a mystery. He is a friend of Prince Harry’s, with whom he shares a commitment to charities that support veterans and military personnel. Apparently, the businessman would be happy to continue hosting the prince, Meghan, and their children for a long time to come. Several theories have circulated regarding the benefactor’s identity, with some speculating that he is Ian Wace, a British financier with an estimated net worth of $1.2 billion and who has long been close to Harry. He owns the Rowler Estate, a vast estate in the Cotswolds. His private life has been marked by tragedy: In 1994 he lost his first wife, Joanna, and their two young children in a car accident in Hampshire.

However, being hosted by a wealthy friend is nothing new in the Sussexes’ lives. In 2020, when they decided to step back from their royal duties and move to the United States, the couple stayed at the Beverly Hills mansion of producer and media mogul Tyler Perry. It was a Tuscan-style residence with eight bedrooms and 12 bathrooms, located within the gated community of Beverly Ridge Estates.

A few months later, in August of that same year, Harry and Meghan purchased a mansion in Montecito, California, where they settled. Surrounded by greenery, the mansion is located in a residential area frequented by some of Hollywood’s most famous stars, including Oprah Winfrey, Ariana Grande, and Brad Pitt. It is a very luxurious home that, at the time of purchase, was dubbed the Sussexes’ new palace—one the couple seems to have no intention of selling, despite their return to the United Kingdom. According to reports, the maintenance staff had continued to care for the family’s chickens.

The couple is still holding on to the California property, purchased for around $14 million, which continues to serve as one of their family homes. The estate includes a wine cellar, a movie theater, a gym, a spa, a large swimming pool, a tennis court, a wood-fired oven, a barbecue, and more than 13 and a half bathrooms.

However, this is not the only residence owned by the Sussexes. Just several years ago, Harry and Meghan purchased a home on the Portuguese coast, near the one owned by Princess Eugenie—Harry’s cousin—and her husband, Jack Brooksbank. The property is located within the CostaTerra Golf & Ocean Club, an exclusive residential complex with about 300 ocean-view villas in Melides, south of Lisbon.

Meanwhile, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are expected in Brussels on November 10 for an event dedicated to protecting children from online risks and abuse. The heart of the initiative, organized by MEP Antonio López-Istúriz White as part of a parliamentary intergroup, will be the unveiling of The Lost Screen Memorial, a video installation created in memory of children who lost their lives after falling victim to online abuse and exploitation. The installation will consist of 50 large-scale portraits of the young victims. European Parliament president Roberta Metsola is also expected to attend the ceremony.

According to reports in the British media, Harry and Meghan will deliver a joint speech on the issue—which has long been a focus of the couple’s advocacy—before participating in a discussion with international activists. Among the scheduled speakers is Sandra Spitaels, the Belgian mother of Glenn, who, in 2017, took his own life at age 15 after a nude photograph of him was circulated online.

These two developments involving the Duke and Duchess of Sussex come as Meghan’s father, Thomas Markle, is at the center of a horrific legal case. He is the subject of an investigation launched following a complaint filed by his son, Thomas Markle Jr., with the Philippine police and the FBI. The younger Thomas handed over to investigators a box containing several images and videos that allegedly depicted child sexual abuse, found among his father’s personal belongings in Cebu City, Philippines.

Another discovery reportedly took place in recent days at a storage unit that Thomas Markle allegedly rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico. The facility was reportedly inspected by local police as part of an investigative operation. Meghan’s 82-year-old father has reportedly been transferred in recent days to a facility in Florida that specializes in caring for people with dementia, according to The Sun.

His move to a care facility could now complicate the investigation, particularly the possibility of questioning Thomas Markle. His cognitive condition could make it more difficult to proceed with the investigation, especially given the protections afforded to residents of specialized facilities.

Meghan, who has had no contact with her father since 2018, has not commented on the latest developments. It had previously emerged that the duchess, who had been aware of the allegations against her father since 2018, wanted to speak out publicly. One of the agents from Royalty and Specialist Protection (RaSP)—the Scotland Yard unit responsible for the security of members of the royal family and other public figures—reportedly advised her not to speak out. The agent reportedly told her, “Leave it with us, we’ll investigate it.”

Thomas Markle was arrested in Florida on Friday on charges connected to the possession of child sexual abuse material. He has previously denied possession of such material.

#3569. 5 Years Ago: Benedict Cumberbatch Starred In Netflix's Best Western Movie

Jane Campion's 2021 film "The Power of the Dog," released five years ago this month, was one of the best films of its year. It was widely praised by critics and by the Academy, despite earning a tiny handful of cash during its not-very-wide theatrical release. The film was nominated for an astonishing 12 Academy Awards, including Best Picture, making it the seventh Netflix film in four years to be nominated in the top category (other nominees included "Roma," "The Irishman," "Marriage Story," "Mank," "The Trial of the Chicago 7," and "Don't Look Up"). "The Power of the Dog" ultimately only won one Oscar, for Best Director.

The film takes place on a ranch in Montana in the mid-1920s, owned by brothers Phil and George Burbank (Benedict Cumberbatch and Jesse Plemons). Kirsten Dunst plays Rose, the proprietress of a local inn, who is raising her teenage son Peter (Kodi Smit-McPhee) by herself. Early in the film, Phil admires that Rose's dining tables are decorated with paper flowers, but becomes a little grossed out when he learns that Peter was the one who constructed them. This little observation kicks off the movie's powerful themes about traditional masculinity, gender dynamics, and the place of queerness on the open frontier.

These four characters get swirled together when George marries Rose and Phil's cruel nature reveals itself. While the young Peter leaves to go to medical school, Rose finds herself under pressure — more from Phil than from George — to be a "woman of the house." Phil insists, for instance, that Rose play the piano at a fancy dinner party, something she can't bear to do. By the time Peter comes home for a break, Rose has begun to hit the bottle.

We soon learn that both Phil and the young Peter are likely queer. Peter is more openly so, as he becomes fascinated by a secret stash of magazines full of hunky dudes. Phil, meanwhile, is very fond of a scarf that once belonged to the now-dead Bronco Henry, his former mentor ... and possibly more. Eventually, Phil begins to take Peter under his wing. Later in the film, Phil tacitly admits that Bronco Henry once saved his life during a blizzard by holding their nude bodies together. It's all but stated outright that Phil and Bronco Henry were lovers. This is the 1920s in rural Montana, however, so these men don't seem to have the freedom, nor even the vocabulary, to express their queerness.

At home, meanwhile, Rose's life is falling apart. She's drinking more and more, and her relationship with Phil is fraught. Although Phil eventually warms to Peter, he seems to place all his self-hate onto Rose, mocking her and making her life as miserable as possible. Phil is blaming Rose, it seems, for forcing him to reckon with his attraction to men. This leads to a late-film twist about rope-making and anthrax that leaves the film on a very dark note indeed.

"The Power of the Dog" is a marvelous tragedy of pain, self-denial, and gender roles. Rose cannot be the "sweet little wife," and Phil masks his need to be gentle and "soft" by affecting a "grizzled" exterior. Cumberbatch is fantastic in the role of Phil, capturing both his character's cruelty and his hidden gentleness. The film's title comes from Psalms, 22:20: "Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs."

Jane Campion's filmography is full of bangers, going back to her early films like "Sweetie" and "An Angel at My Table," through "The Piano" and "Portrait of a Lady," and up to "Bright Star" and "The Power of the Dog." This has been her most recent film to date.

Critics loved this movie, which earned a 94% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes based on 363 reviews. /Film wrote that Cumberbatch delivered a career-best performance. Meanwhile, The New York Times' Manohla Dargis loved the sweep of the film as well as its treatment of the Phil character, a man who, she observed, had been "playing" a cowboy for decades of his life. About the film's visuals, Dargis wrote:

"A bold visual stylist, Campion introduces this world and its people with sweep and precision, with soaring eagle-eye aerial shots and her characteristic attention to voluptuary detail (and with New Zealand doubling for an unspoiled Montana). She fluently sets the western milieu, with its swirling dust and thundering cattle, and catches the boisterous camaraderie of the ranch hands, the playfulness of their jostling with its easy, unselfconscious physicality and intimacy."

/Film's Joshua Meyer wrote a full explanation of the ending of "The Power of the Dog," realizing that it's a tale of emotional terrorism and that it may be freeing to wriggle out from under the masculine lifestyle Phil was trying to perpetuate. "The Power of the Dog" was based on the novel by Thomas Savage, and Campion, who also wrote the adaptation, changed the ending (we think for the better). In Campion's version, the themes are incredibly clear, very moving, and pointedly righteous.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3567. Vija Celmins, the Ultimate Artist’s Artist, Gets Honored by LACMA

On Wednesday, I walked down Crosby Street and stopped at an easy-to-miss building where, high above the cobblestoned street, is the studio of Vija Celmins, who’s been there for almost 50 years. It’s a classic gigantic SoHo artist loft, the kind you’ll be shocked to hear still exist—but they do. In the 1970s, the previous tenant put a Buddhist temple in the front room. Not finding anything particularly wrong with that, Celmins lived in the temple for a while.

“Then I finally thought, gee, maybe I could put a couch in here,” Celmins told me as I walked in.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s been decades since the galleries moved from SoHo to Chelsea and got replaced by boutiques. But among this warren of cast iron buildings, some of the artists who moved in during the pioneer days remain. Among them is Celmins, the masterful pop-landscapist who paints in infinite textures, taking on the universal with an obsessive tenacity. The 88-year-old is a living link to a long-gone generation, and someone always in the running when we talk about the best artists who are both still with us and who began their careers before the JFK assassination.

Approaching nonagenarian status, Celmins is still incredibly quick, with a generous, buoyant voice. She immediately hopped down the stairs of her old studio and took me over to the windows.

“I used to be able to see down the street before they built this ugly pink building—all the way to the bridge, because this was a parking lot,” she told me, referring to a building erected 21 years ago.

She walked past a print she made some years ago: a depiction of the ocean, her most famous subject, installed on the wall. She admired it in a refreshingly objective way.

“It’s so loose. Usually I tighten everything down,” she said. “I mean, it’s such a relief. I had forgotten that. And what did I do? I only made 10 of them, which is interesting, in ’16. I must have done this at… It looks like it’s a drypoint—doesn’t it look like drypoint? I mean, I did a fucking lot of oceans, as you know.”

Though not a household name, in certain circles, Celmins has attained near-mythic status. The very few people I told about this interview ahead of time were shocked she was having anyone over to her studios in Manhattan and Long Island. She works incredibly slowly, and thus has shown incredibly infrequently. This has started to change in the last few years. She had a retrospective at the Met Breuer in 2019, and in the last few years, a few shows of new work at her gallery, Matthew Marks—the blue-chip commercial concern that represents a disproportionate number of the greatest American artists.

Next year, Celmins will have a show at Dia Bridgehampton. Tomorrow, she’s the guest of honor at the LACMA Art+Film Gala, a big deal in American museumdom. It comes with a gigantic bash presided over by Leonardo DiCaprio and Eva Chow. The gala’s also honoring Denis Villeneuve, which Celmins is excited about. She’s seen the Dune movies and, like Villeneuve, is a big fan of the desert.

During my visit, she opened up a random drawer under a drawing table. There was stuff everywhere, decades of sketches and notes and Post-its. She has a constellation of postcards taped to the wall, with paintings as inspiration, ones that look nothing like Vija Celmins—Picasso, Balthus—along with photos of her heroes and her friends with pets. There’s Jasper Johns with his dog, Borges with his cat. She’s got framed artworks from friends who are mostly dead now, like a Ken Price drawing of some undulating cups—“You know Kenny Price?”—and a very kooky, absolutely amazing H.C. Westermann of a wolf with its heart throbbing in its chest, wandering through the desert. Westermann made it for her. She made Westermann a wolf drawing in return. She doesn’t know what happened to her wolf.

There are drawings of globes, sculptures of globes, her tablet paintings, more prints of the ocean, a paperweight from an insurance company in Kansas City—near where she grew up in Indiana after leaving Latvia—a wrapped-up canvas labeled “ED MOSES” on the side, and plenty of drawings of Saturn.

She moved into the SoHo place after two decades working in Venice Beach, California. While in LA, she honed and refined, and inarguably mastered, a painstakingly laborious practice of applying graphite to paper in slow, methodical marks, rendering the passage of time in hyperreal landscapes. She now mostly works in a studio on the eastern end of Long Island, where she's had a place for the last few decades. But it’s here at the SoHo studio, in the erstwhile cauldron of cutting-edge American art, where she loves to be.

“The studio out in the country is more like where I went back to painting, really,” she told me. “And here I did all these weird things.”

This wasn’t the first time we had met. A few weeks back, I was admiring the very cool Gary Hume show that Marks had up in his gallery on 24th Street when gallery director Jacqueline Tran tapped me on the shoulder and asked if I would like to meet Vija Celmins. Vija Celmins! At the public opening!

We chatted for a few moments. She seemed spry, fit, with an elastic mind. Then she invited me over for lunch—not in the city, but at her place on farmland out east. On an October morning I hopped on a Jitney, then an Uber to Celmins’s part of the hamlet, which is essentially rural, with small clapboard homes encircled by crop formations.

I arrived at the same time as my fellow visitors: Michael Govan, the director of LACMA, and his wife, the fashion executive Katherine Ross. Celmins welcomed us in and introduced us to her cat, Raymond, who immediately pounced on my cup of takeout coffee.

“Down, Raymond! He’s very friendly,” Celmins said. “He’s my son.”

Out here, in the two-room studio attached to her house, she’s been able to conjure a vision of landscape perhaps more potent than the breakthroughs she came to so many years ago. In her studio, she showed us how the raindrops on her window, as captured in her work-intensive flattened plane panorama, could take on epic qualities.

We sat down for lunch—quiche and soup from a local bakery—and Celmins started telling stories about California. She hadn’t lived there in a number of years, though the topography of the state is what willed her artwork into being. She drove out to the desert with James Turrell, with Doug Wheeler, and spent years—decades—arguing with Robert Irwin, who taught her at UCLA. Irwin called Celmins his “star student.” I’ve always liked this Bob Irwin quote about Celmins: “Vija has perfect taste. She doesn’t like anything.”

Govan told her about the museum, LACMA, and the new building that had finally been completed earlier this year after two decades of planning and fundraising. Celmins was quite curious about it all. She has a few plans for when she’s in town for the LACMA gala. She seemed intrigued about meeting her fellow honoree, director Villeneuve, and watched the Dune movies in preparation. (I heartily recommended she watch Sicario and Arrival as well.) She’s going to visit her old studio at 701 Venice Boulevard, which she hasn’t seen in decades.

“I was going to go out in the desert, but I’m not going to have time to do it,” she said. “I might have to make another trip. I really like the Death Valley desert because it’s so vast, so terrific. And they have airplanes zooming from the Air Force around really fast. I used to wave at them. They go really low, and they just go like, vvvvvrrroooooom! Right above, following the outline of the mountains.”

She’s also going to see Riko Mizuno, her Los Angeles art dealer, who is currently 94 years old. But most of her friends are gone.

“A lot of them have died, I mean, I didn’t have that many friends, but some died, and some are dying right now,” she said. “And then they moved away. Ed Moses, I knew pretty well. Billy Al Bengston. Well, Kenny Price, I loved Kenny.”

Then she mentioned Robert Therrien—“You know Bob Therrien?”—the late artist who has become quite famous for oversized sculptures that are astronomically popular on Instagram. A retrospective at The Broad this year became something of a sensation. I can’t imagine an artist more different than Celmins—but as it turns out, they had a deep mutual respect for each other.

“I met him once, and he was a very unusual person,” Celmins said. “He was really tall, and everything in his studio was like—he had a ceiling that was maybe like 25, 28 feet tall. And he had this little ladder that went up this side to this kitchen, which was this kitchen he remade from Chicago or someplace where his family used to live. I’ll show you one little thing. He gave me this.”

She got up from her chair and found the Therrian artwork on a shelf. It was a snout, bobbing up and down in a terrifying manner, attached to a curved metal rod. Just the inner part of the face of a canine, floating forever.

“It’s so disorienting. Where’s the rest of the dog?” I asked.

Since Jodie Sweetin and Andrea Barber launched their Full House rewatch podcast, How Rude, Tanneritos!, plenty of BTS sitcom tea has been spilled. From the fact that producers had a preferred Olsen twin to work with to the anger on set when Candace Cameron Bure cut her hair without warning, there's been so much to learn about the TGIF show. And, on the latest podcast episode, it was revealed that one actor had “too big a pack” to be wearing biker shorts for a scene with Kimmy Gibbler, and this sounds so cringey.

In the season 7 episode of “Love on the Rocks,” DJ Tanner debates whether or not to break up with her boyfriend, Steve Hale. When she goes mountain climbing with Kimmy and her boyfriend, Keanu, she gains a new perspective on her life and relationship. While discussing the episode, in a recent episode of How Rude, Tanneritos!, Kimmy actress Andrea Barber exposed a rather revealing detail about her on-screen boyfriend that cropped up amid filming:

This poor actor, Keanu. So originally, he wasn’t wearing his jacket and it was just his shirt and his biker shorts. But, the bike shorts were a little tight. And a little too revealing.

Yes, poor actor! When you rewatch the episode, the biker shorts Keanu was wearing really did look tight, almost like spandex. And for a family-friendly show, it makes sense to cover that up. Like Sweetin humorously said, that’s just too much information for families at home to see.

It’s common for wardrobe changes to happen when an actor on a family-friendly sitcom is showing a little growth down there. That happened to Jaleel White when he was asked to hide his bulge in Family Matters. In the case of Brian Evans, who played Keanu, Barber explained that the wardrobe department had other ideas to hide that area:

They got a note. Costumes got a note from Video Village. And so, they had to quickly find this jacket. A long jacket to cover.

Well, I’ve got to say, the long jacket worked. You can’t see anything. Hey, you do what you have to do to keep the Full House episode G-rated.

Anyone curious as to how Brian Evans felt about the embarrassing wardrobe change should know he told EW that he “didn’t know what was happening.” Not only that, but he also revealed the priceless reaction his mother had when one of the crew members told him he had “too big of a pack" for a teenager on this show”:

I remember seeing my mother’s face sitting at the studio audience just beet red, laughing.

This certainly isn't the kind of moment I would've expected to hear regarding the long-binge-watchable show, but it's also a funny piece of information. Thank goodness the costume department of the ABC sitcom was right on top of it. Otherwise, I could imagine the producers receiving some not-so-flattering letters from parents.

It’ll be hard not to think about this little (or not-so-little) tidbit of information when watching this Full House episode moving forward. Still, the detail shouldn't be too distracting for audiences given how the jacket comes into play. Fans can watch “Love on the Rocks” and more episodes of the show by streaming them with either a Hulu subscription or a Disney+ subscription.
