#3529. The Johnny Depp Comeback Hits Judgment Day with ‘Ebenezer’: How Paramount Is Carefully Reintroducing the Controversial Star

Hollywood studios turned away Johnny Depp eight years ago. With “Ebenezer,” Paramount Pictures is betting that audiences have not rejected him too. The “A Christmas Carol” adaptation, out November 13, marks a decisive moment for the studio, as it was one of the first films boarded by the company after its 2025 acquisition by Skydance.

Depp got some positive social media attention Monday evening when he was filmed “wyling out” and “wreaking havoc” in the Christmas Market of New York’s Bryant Park — as Scrooge, of course. In his first major pre-release promotional stop for “Ebenezer,” Depp donned a fright wig and make-up to enact some staged bah-humbugging, which included popping balloons, knocking over a Christmas tree, and playfully antagonizing an on-site Santa Claus. The stunt was Depp’s second in-character appearance as Scrooge, coming three months after a similarly interactive appearance at San Diego Comic-Con that also generated mounds of social media content from passerby. Later on at the event, Scrooge appeared onstage during Collider’s Directors on Directing panel to debut the first “Ebenezer” trailer. Related Stories Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money The Bay Theater in Palisades Village, Closed Since the LA Wildfires, Will Reopen Thanks to Paramount and Rick Caruso

The approach leans into how audiences know Depp, who became one of the industry’s biggest stars in the aughts with his quirked-up performances in the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise and various Tim Burton joints. But several publicity veterans note that it’s also a strategy that helps the star skirt addressing himself: a typical component to the modern promotional gauntlet of podcast appearances and junketing. Paramount and representatives for Depp declined to comment for this story.

Indeed, the last time Depp was promoting a blockbuster in character was at Warner Bros.’ San Diego Comic-Con panel in 2018, where he appeared as Gellert Grindelwald, the seductively authoritarian wizard within J.K. Rowling’s world of “Harry Potter,” to promote the second “Fantastic Beasts” prequel. Depp was mired in controversy at the time, as his ex-wife, Amber Heard, alleged that he had been “physically abusive” in court documents filed in their divorce case. Depp denied the claims. Making things more awkward — Heard appeared at the same studio presentation, popping up an hour later for a panel hyping “Aquaman.”

Two years later, Depp departed from a third (and what ended up to be the final) “Fantastic Beasts” entry. On Instagram, the actor posted that he had been “asked to resign” by the studio. Depp had just lost a U.K. libel trial against The Sun, in which a judge ruled that an article reporting that the actor was a “wife beater” was found to be “substantially true.”

But Depp later claimed victory in a U.S. defamation trial against Heard herself. Heard had written a Washington Post op-ed in which she described herself as a survivor of domestic abuse. Depp claimed the article damaged his reputation and career; both parties argued the other was the aggressor through the grueling six-week spectacle. An initial jury ruling sided with Depp on three separate claims of defamation, ordering Heard pay him $10.35 million in damages. Heard won on one of her three counterclaims of defamation, ordering Depp to pay her $2 million. A later appeal by Heard ended with a settlement in which she agreed to pay $1 million to Depp.

The highly-gawked-at and internet-scrutinized trial reignited his fame and infamy, depending on your perspective. Once a big-screen titan, he was now ubiquitous on social media, particularly TikTok, emerging with an ardent online fanbase forged by a conviction that he was a man who had been rashly cast aside during the #MeToo movement’s prominence in the late 2010’s.

With “Ebenezer,” Paramount has the unique assignment of capitalizing on that celebrity, without inviting relitigation of an ugly legal battle that would cloud the sunny promotion of a family feature. Hence, the in-character appearances, along with underlining Depp’s penchant for transformative turns (though no further ones are planned). A promotional video featuring snippets of cast interviews, including the likes of Ian McKellen, Daisy Ridley, and Tramell Tillman, praise the actor as giving “a performance the likes of which you’ve never seen before.”

“A less clever route would be turning the release into a ‘comeback’ victory lap. The result could be an unnecessary and noisy polarization of views, reviving the very controversy the studio would prefer to move beyond,” says media lawyer and crisis manager Amber Melville-Brown, who heads the media and reputation team at the law firm Withers. “A campaign built around vindication invites an argument about who, precisely, has been vindicated and for what — starting the debate over again. A campaign built around the performance sparks a different conversation.”

Meanwhile, Paramount has been careful to show “Ebenezer” to select audiences so far. The film was unveiled Sunday in New York City with a “special screening” at the Whitby Hotel’s 147-seat screening room — an intimate venue for the first unveiling of a studio feature. A handful of press outlets and more influencers were invited to a small carpet. One front-facing video posted by a guest featured her meeting Depp and calling the occasion “my sign from God that I chose the right path today.” A London premiere will take place at Odeon Luxe Leicester Square on Monday.

In another shrewd booking, Depp made a surprise onstage appearance during Aerosmith’s Hollywood Bowl concert on October 29. While other actors may tap in for a late-night spot or “Hot Ones” interview to mark the home stretch of film promotion, Depp instead let a guitar solo on “Train Kept A-Rollin'” do the talking.

Down the line, the “Ebenezer” review embargo will lift November 12, mere hours before public screenings begin — almost always a sign that a studio has little confidence in finding good PR from the critic class. The film’s director, Ti West, has usually drawn positive reviews through his career, mostly known as an indie horror darling until this first studio feature.

But most importantly for Paramount, “Ebenezer” doesn’t need to be a blockbuster to find success. The film’s production budget netted out to a rather modest $38 million, giving it a much easier pathway to theatrical profitability than Depp’s previous mega-budget tentpoles. Along with that comes hopes to leg out through the holiday season and a bank on grosses from overseas territories, where other older male movie stars like Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise have better retained their ability to sell tickets.

Rival studios are looking closely at whether audiences still see Depp as a big screen draw. Lionsgate is already in the Depp business for the revenge thriller “Day Drinker,” releasing in March. And at Disney’s D23 Expo in August, “Pirates of the Caribbean” producer Jerry Bruckheimer floated hopes to get the star on board for a sixth installment. That franchise has laid dormant for nearly a decade, despite numerous reports of development teams tinkering on a Depp-less take. In one of the more interesting quotes from the “Ebenezer” event in New York, Depp spoke with Entertainment Tonight and slid in a dig at the 2017 entry “Dead Men Tell No Tales,” saying he’d be open to a franchise return but noting that “the only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note.”

But when Depp was first jettisoned from Hollywood’s A-list, major studios had begun to tire of his antics. There were reports of erratic on-set behavior, sky-high salary demands, and — in the true offender for studios — diminishing box office returns. The “Pirates” films still made money, but Depp headlined several costly bombs, including “Alice Through the Looking Glass” and “Mortdecai,” which had left companies less eager to write big checks, particularly given his public relations scandals.

But Depp’s absence may have not curbed his following. A National Research Group study from earlier this year found that he was the seventh-most cited name by people, especially in Europe, when they wre asked to name five actors or actresses that would motivate them to see “a new movie in a cinema,” even though he’s been away from the big screen for nearly a decade. Over those years, a growing refrain in the business has been that some movie stars have kneecapped their ability to open films by signing on to streaming productions, curbing consumers’ association of them with theaters. In that context, Depp may prove to be a unicorn, having essentially sat out years of the industry chasing Netflix — even if it wasn’t his choice to.

#3528. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3527. All 4 Cillian Murphy Performances In Christopher Nolan Movies, Ranked

Like many filmmakers, Christopher Nolan often works with the same actors across different projects. Sir Michael Caine has appeared in eight Nolan films total. In second place, with room to eventually become no. 1 given Caine's retirement, is Cillian Murphy.

Murphy has acted in six films directed by Nolan, in chronological order: "Batman Begins," "The Dark Knight," "Inception," "The Dark Knight Rises," "Dunkirk," and their shared magnum opus "Oppenheimer." This prosperous creative relationship all started when Murphy auditioned to play Bruce Wayne in "Batman Begins." The two recall that they both knew Murphy wasn't the right pick for the Dark Knight, but Murphy's acting impressed Nolan enough that he fought, and won, to cast Murphy instead as one of the movie's villains: Doctor Jonathan Crane, the Scarecrow.

Since then, Nolan has always known just the right way to use Murphy, to the point you could call the actor his secret weapon. Until "Oppenheimer," Murphy had never played the lead in a Nolan movie, but the director always cast him in important supporting roles (ones that needed the right actor or the whole film around them would suffer). With "Oppenheimer," Murphy carried the entire movie on his back, and his previous Nolan film performances show why he had earned the trust needed for that casting.

Even Cillian Murphy's smallest role in a Christopher Nolan movie still has meat on the bones. Nolan's World War II film "Dunkirk" depicts the 1940 evacuation of British troops from the eponymous French shoreline. Murphy plays one of those thousands of troops, specifically one whose boat gets destroyed by a German U-Boat. He's rescued by a civilian ship volunteering as a rescue boat, but taking that ride means sailing back into the carnage he just escaped.

Murphy's character doesn't even have a name, being known only as "the Shivering Soldier." Pulled from the cold water by Mr. Dawson (Mark Rylance) and boys Peter (Tom Glynn-Carney) and George (Barry Keoghan), he indeed shivers, wrapping himself in a blanket onboard. The soldier already counts himself one of the lucky ones for surviving, and he refuses to let the ship continue heading towards Dunkirk, which he believes is certain death.

With the terrifying scene the movie paints of the battle, it's hard to dismiss the soldier's fears. Peter asks if the soldier is a coward, but Mr. Dawson counters he's only shell-shocked. Murphy can pull off a thousand-yard stare like few other actors can (something he'd again do to great effect in "Oppenheimer"). That silent and haunted quality he can project makes him perfect for this part: A man who stared death in the face while watching it work all around him ... and is now being asked to do so again after getting no time to recover.

Cillian Murphy's Scarecrow is the only villain to appear in all three of the "Dark Knight Trilogy" films. During "Batman Begins," Jonathan Crane, reimagined as the head of Arkham Asylum, is in bed with both the mob and the League of Shadows, who plot to destroy Gotham City with Crane's fear toxin. Crane then returns for cameos in "The Dark Knight," being captured by Batman (Christian Bale), and "The Dark Knight Rises," serving as a judge in Bane's (Tom Hardy) kangaroo court.

Murphy is relishing playing a super-villain without ever going into pure camp territory. Though Dr. Crane admittedly isn't physically imposing, his frosty blue-eyed gaze still makes him look like a guy who can and would kill you. He's even the first villain to get one over on Batman, dosing the Dark Knight with his fear toxin and setting him on fire. Crane does the last part with a cruel quip befitting his psychologist background: "You look like a man who takes himself too seriously. Do you want my opinion? You need to lighten up."

Crane is both a sadist and a psychologist obsessed with studying the effects of fear. He relishes putting people on edge, particularly pesky crusading lawyer Rachel Dawes (Katie Holmes). But Murphy's best Scarecrow scene is definitely when he pulls rank on imprisoned mob boss Carmine Falcone (Tom Wilkinson). Murphy completely changes the tenor of the scene with Crane's line: "Would you like to see my mask?" It instantly shows Crane is not some mere corrupt bureaucrat.

Scarecrow always shows a catty sense of humor, too. So, it's fitting that his last scene in the trilogy is sentencing Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman), and others who refuse to choose between "death or exile," to "death — by exile."

In between "Dark Knight" movies, Christopher Nolan and Cillian Murphy made a little film you might've heard of called "Inception." It's a heist/con movie, but it's set inside a dreamscape. Murphy plays the dreamer and the crew's mark: Robert Fischer, the heir to an oil empire reeling from the death of his disapproving father (Pete Postlethwaite). Dominic Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his crew are hired by Fischer's rival, Mr. Saito (Ken Watanabe), to plant an idea inside his head that'll make him resolve to break up his father's empire instead of inheriting it.

Speaking to Irish Central in 2010, Murphy mentioned he researched the sons of Rupert Murdoch to understand how being raised in a titan of industry's shadow would shape someone (and this was well before "Succession" gave us a Murdoch roman à clef). Murphy added that he played Fischer as "a petulant child who's in need of a lot of attention from his father." But while "Inception" is all about tricking Fischer, the movie isn't unsympathetic to him.

"Inception" is widely read as an allegory for filmmaking itself. Fischer is the audience, the one who needs to be deceived by the craft and illusion, to believe that something is real in their gut even when their brain knows it isn't. The entire movie hinges on the titular inception, where Fischer sees an illusion of his father on his deathbed and gets what life denied him: reassurance that his dad did care about him. And just as the inception has to convince Fischer, Murphy has to convince us of the emotional sincerity. An overwhelmed Fischer tears up, and as his face crumbles, it's hard not to get a lump in your own throat. It's extra painful since it's all a falsehood.

"Oppenheimer" cleaned house at the 96th Oscars, including Cillian Murphy winning Best Actor for playing the father of the atomic bomb — or, as Oppenheimer infamously called himself later in life, "death, destroyer of worlds."

On the surface, it's a transformative performance. Murphy lost weight to better capture the gaunt Oppenheimer's physique, and he completely re-modulated his voice. (Murphy based his soft but deep and rhythmic baritone as Oppenheimer on a combination of Orson Welles and Fred Rogers). But despite those hallmarks of actor transformation, the kind that often feel cynically used to win an Oscar, Murphy as Oppenheimer isn't gaudy acting. No, it's more like a chameleon shifting into a new color: Murphy becomes Oppenheimer, utterly.

"Oppie" may have been eccentric, but "Oppenheimer" is much more interested in exploring how his foibles led to his downfall — and perhaps humanity's — than venerating them as the cost of his scientific know-how. Oppenheimer is willfully naive about how the bomb he's building will be used and pathologically incapable of taking too strong a stand on anything. His equivocation often only digs him deeper. Indeed, Murphy excels in scenes that show the weighty consequences of Oppenheimer's awkwardness, like when he meets with violently anticommunist Colonel Pash (Casey Affleck) or stumbles while urging U.S. President Harry Truman (Gary Oldman) to push for nuclear de-escalation.

Oppenheimer seeking absolution from Truman by talking about the "blood on [his] hands" makes it hard to disagree with Lewis Strauss' (Robert Downey Jr.) argument that Oppenheimer wanted to be both the maker of the bomb and a martyr for its destructiveness. But in Murphy's moments of silent stillness (particularly the ending when his character imagines the world's fiery end), he shows how Oppenheimer's guilt, though self-inflicted, was all too real and impossibly heavy to carry.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has finally released, and by all accounts is one of the best-reviewed games of the year so far. Fortunately, there's more Zelda to come, thanks to the fans.

As a ROM hack (a modified version of a video game) of the original Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, The Legend of Zelda: Indigo takes place 27-years after the events of The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask and offers players a unique new take set in the beloved Nintendo universe.

The game has been in development since 2022 by Kenton M and their small team of volunteers, so you'd be forgiven for assuming it was one of the many overly ambitious fan projects that will probably never see the light of day. However, developer Kenton M recently shared an update on YouTube showing off some of the game's areas. It looks like an impressively creepy world, too.

While Kenton M and team previously suggested the game might end up releasing before GTA 6, Rockstar's juggernaut open-world crime sim arrives November 19, and I don't reckon Indigo will suddenly materialize in the next two weeks. Even so, this one really does look worth the wait, using Ocarina of Time's engine to build something completely new.

In The Legend of Zelda: Indigo we play as an older, bearded Hero of Time. Players can also expect brand-new items and weapons along with a brand-new dialogue system which aims to make for more rewarding, in-depth characters and quests. "This is going to allow us to really lean into the story and side quests," Kenton M explains. Not only that, but it'll support the developer's goal to have player choices actually have an impact upon the world.

As far as ROM hacks go, this is definitely one of the more impressive ones I've seen, and I'm really curious to see more. For now, though, we can all fall in love with Ocarina of Time all over again. In our own 9/10 review, we called the game a loving remake that we wished would take just a few more risks.

"The Switch 2 remake preserves its legacy, though it resists change in ways that occasionally clash. Remakes are always a sticky subject: many fans want the game to be completely different, while others want it to be basically the same, but on a modern platform with easy access. There's no real solution to making a remake that satisfies everyone, but Ocarina of Time comes close. With some additional content and replay value, it could easily have been the definitive version. But it will "just" have to settle for being an incredible remake that's worth playing at least once. Ocarina of Time is arguably worth playing in any iteration, including Switch 2."

#3525. Zelda: Ocarina of Time Beats The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim in One Major Way

After years spent dreaming of a remake or remaster of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, the highest-rated video game of all time according to Metacritic, fans finally saw their wish fulfilled in 2026. Nintendo announced a remake for Switch 2 earlier this year, and the title arrived in stores this week.

Nintendo has taken some heat for relying on remakes and remasters to bolster the Switch 2 library, but time after time, they seem to delight fans and earn favorable critical reviews. Such positive performance suggests the remakes ought to continue, at least for now. It also highlights one major way Ocarina of Time beats other games that have received numerous releases over the years, such as The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim.

Depending on how you count it, Skyrim has appeared on 13 unique platforms as of November 2026, including Google Stadia (since shut down) and Amazon Alexa. There have been VR editions and bundles gathering fan-created content and expansion packs. The game originally launched on Nov. 10, 2011, and since then, it has appeared almost everywhere a large audience exists.

For its part, Ocarina of Time has appeared on far fewer platforms since its debut in 1998. That comparative rarity means each new version feels like an event, as we see with the anticipation and hype surrounding Ocarina of Time in 2026.

After it was released on the Nintendo 64, Ocarina of Time got two ports for the GameCube in North America. Nintendo included it as part of The Legend of Zelda: Collector’s Edition, a bundle of four games from the series that also included Majora’s Mask and the original NES entries, along with a demo for The Wind Waker. It also headlined a separate compilation that included the Master Quest, which previously had been available only on the Nintendo 64DD in Japan.

Next came The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time 3D in June 2011 for the handheld Nintendo 3DS. It presented the classic adventure with quality-of-life improvements and a 3D visual effect so players could see Hyrule with extra dimension. This version also included improved texture quality throughout the adventure. If you could handle playing on a tiny screen, it was the best way to enjoy that classic version of Hyrule for years.

Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2 includes even more quality-of-life improvements, better controls, and dramatically improved visuals that incorporate an aesthetic we wouldn’t find out of place in a classic volume of fairy tales, or even in a high-end doll shop. Critics consider the game one of the year’s finest, awarding it a current Metacritic score of 96 out of 100.

There was no guarantee Nintendo could produce that result. Ocarina of Time is generally considered one of the finest games of all time, but some players find its mechanics dated. Some people just don’t like Zelda all that much. And so on, and so forth. Despite those obstacles, the development team pulled through and the result of their labor seems to be pleasing both returning fans and newcomers who have stepped into Hyrule for the very first time.

Compare that stellar reception to the one that accompanies yet another new version of Skyrim, and the difference is clear. Bethesda simply doesn’t give players time to miss the game that has accounted for more sales than any other in the company’s history. There’s always a new version of Skyrim waiting just around the corner, it seems. Perhaps we’ll even see another few editions launch before we finally get our hands on The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

New Skyrim ports usually bring genuine enhancements, but they tend to be minor if you’ve already played the original game and its expansions. Humorously, one of the most interesting versions of the game came to Nintendo hardware with Zelda-related content, starting with the Switch in November 2017. Players could dress like Link by acquiring the Champion’s Tunic, and equip themselves with the Master Sword and Hylian Shield.

I don’t mind seeing companies release multiple versions of the games players love most, because it makes them accessible to a wider audience. They also prevent me from having to haul out all my old consoles the next time I’m in a retro mood. But the slew of releases can grow tiresome when they are priced as premium titles but don’t add content or meaningful improvements. Ocarina of Time, the crown jewel in Nintendo’s library, has avoided that fate. Skyrim, the best thing Bethesda has built and launched so far, has not.

#3524. Michael Fassbender's Underrated 2015 Western Is Worth Revisiting

Lots of modern Westerns take the adventurous romance out of the genre, like director John Maclean's 2015 "Slow West." A major hit at the 2015 Sundance Film Festival, it won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize in the Dramatic category, and then made its way into theaters (with a simultaneous video-on-demand release). More than a decade on, "Slow West" remains one of the best Westerns of this century. And you can watch it on Netflix right now — although it's leaving soon, so act fast. It's also free, with ads, on YouTube.

"Slow West" lives up to its title with a leisurely pace, but it's also a tight 84-minute movie. In 19th century Colorado, a young Scottish man named Jay Cavendish (Kodi Smit-McPhee) sets off in search of his supposed one true love, Rose (Caren Pistorius) — who left Scotland with a price on her head. Jay meets bounty hunter Silas Selleck (Michael Fassbender) by chance and Silas becomes his guide and guardian. They also run afoul of Payne (Ben Mendelsohn), leader of a gang Silas once belonged to; Payne is interested in collecting the bounty on Rose.

Smit-McPhee later appeared in the acclaimed 2021 Western "The Power of the Dog," which similarly paired him up with Benedict Cumberbatch just as "Slow West" does with him and Fassbender. In "The Power of the Dog," Smit-McPhee is a wolf in sheep's clothing, one who weaponizes his unassuming innocence. In "Slow West," that innocence is exactly what you get with Jay Cavendish. He has naive ideas about adventure and love — Rose never actually reciprocated his feelings, but he's convinced the grand gesture of tracking her down will sway her. While the frontier forces him to defend himself with a gun, it's clear throughout the film Jay isn't built for the gunslinging life.

Jay's origins as a Scotsman traveling through America in "Slow West" are almost autobiographical for John Maclean, who is from Scotland himself. (Notably, while the parts of the film set in America were filmed in New Zealand, flashbacks to Scotland were filmed in the real country.) Speaking to the International Business Times in 2015, Maclean said how, when he first decided to write a Western, one of the first "seeds" of the story for him was to depict a frontier filled with European immigrants moving west. Jay and Rose are Scottish, Michael Fassbender uses his Irish accent to play Silas, and (without spoilers) Jay and Silas meet a Swedish family during their travels.

Unlike Jay, a newcomer to America, Maclean had seen plenty of America before making "Slow West" — which was what drew him to the Western: "After college [a few friends and I] took cars through America delivering them. So, I did a lot of traveling in America. That probably led to me wanting to do a Western."

"Slow West" was McLean's first feature film; before that, he'd been a musician and part of a group called The Beta Band, where he played keyboards and directed music videos. According to Maclean, Fassbender agreed to act in his short films because he'd been a fan of those Beta Band videos.

"He was shooting ['Inglourious Basterds'] at the time, so the fact that he even offered his services was a great thing," said Maclean to the BBC. Considering that creative partnership led to "Slow West," one of Michael Fassbender's best movies, the actor's judgment was sound.

#3523. Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52

Sebastián Lelio, the humanistic Chilean filmmaker whose trans drama “A Fantastic Woman” won the Best International Feature Film Oscar in 2018, has died at age 52.

The Chilean publication Emol first revealed the news that he was found dead in his home in Santiago on Friday, November 6, amid an undisclosed health issue. His body was discovered by his partner, the actress/director Amalia Kassai, who starred in his final film, the protest musical “The Wave” from Cannes 2025. Kassai also posted a statement in Spanish on her Instagram account.

Lelio was reportedly mid-production on the feature “Chilean Poet,” adapted from Alejandro Zambra’s Viking-published 2022 novel. Along with “A Fantastic Woman,” he also directed the Hasidic lesbian romance “Disobedience” in the same year, 2017; it starred Rachel McAdams and Rachel Weisz, and helped bring the filmmaker to international prominence. In 2013, he directed Paulina García to a Berlinale Silver Bear Best Actress win with “Gloria,” a late-in-life romantic comedy about a 58-year-old divorcee starting over again. He remade his own film in 2018 in English as “Gloria Bell,” released by A24 and starring Julianne Moore in the role García originated, opposite John Turturro.

Lelio regularly collaborated with the Chilean brothers Pablo Larraín and Juan de Dios Larraín, who served as producers on nearly all of his films. They were also collaborating with Lelio on his ongoing, now-final feature. Born in Argentina, he emigrated to Chile at age two with his mother and later graduated from Chilean Film School, after which he launched his career with short films and music videos. His debut narrative feature, “The Sacred Family,” premiered at the San Sebastián International Film Festival in Spain before his follow-up, “Navidad,” premiered at Cannes in 2009. The post-Chilean-earthquake drama “The Year of the Tiger,” starring beloved Chilean actor Luis Dubó, debuted at Locarno in 2011.

His fourth feature, “Gloria,” shot digitally and with a script and dialogue developed in part with his actors, including García, received U.S. distribution from Roadside Attractions and was widely regarded as one of the best films of 2013.

Lelio directed the first Best International Feature Oscar entry to win the Academy Award with 2017’s Golden Bear-nominated “A Fantastic Woman,” an exuberantly styled drama that put trans actress Daniela Vega on the international map. As Vega consulted on the script, it’s widely seen as a groundbreaker of trans portrayals onscreen in the 21st century. And it helped reform the perception and attitudes toward transness in Lelio and Vega’s home of Chile — and inevitably, within the Academy.

Lelio’s favorite films on the 2022 Sight & Sound poll included “La Dolce Vita,” “Playtime,” “The 400 Blows,” and “Singin’ in the Rain,” and you can feel their impact across his often irreverent, at times burstingly colorful, playful body of work.

His 2017 TIFF premiere “Disobedience” received U.S. distribution from Bleecker Street, and told the story of a forbidden, transgressive romance between two Orthodox Jewish women (McAdams and Weisz) in North London. The tender, taboo drama performed well in North America, grossing nearly $3.5 million domestic during a spring-through-summer 2018 run.

Lelio, that year, deftly remade “Gloria” as “Gloria Bell” with Julianne Moore as the free-spirited divorcee being wooed by John Turturro, and weighing choices in her next chapter living as a yoga instructor in Los Angeles. Returning to filming after the pandemic, Lelio broadened his collaborative scope to adapt “Room” author Emma Donoghue’s “The Wonder,” with Donoghue and Alice Birch co-writing the script with him. Florence Pugh starred as a British nurse sent to Ireland to observe a miraculous “fasting girl,” in a film that played Telluride and streamed on Netflix to strong reviews.

His last film, “The Wave,” took a minute to get off the ground after playing out of competition in Cannes 2025. The story of an introverted music student whose passion for protest is awakened amid a growing feminist movement on campus, “The Wave” received a small release from Wolfe Video earlier this year and received positive response throughout its festival run.

The status of Lelio’s final film isn’t known right now, but we can imagine that Lelio’s sensitive approach to character — and unstable identities finding their footing, their purest expression — will carry into the new work. The Larraín brothers were also producing the film, with Lelio’s regular cinematographer Benjamín Echazarreta on board as DP.

#3522. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3521. One Of Willy Wonka's Most Memorable Scenes Was An Absolute Nightmare To Shoot

Most Gen-Xers know Mel Stuart's 1971 musical movie "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory" by heart and will — perhaps recoiling in disgust — remember the scene where Augustus Gloop (Michael Böllner) falls into a river of chocolate. It seems that moment was equally revolting to film.

The scene in question occurs about halfway through the movie, by which point Willy Wonka (Gene Wilder) has opened the doors to his ultra-secretive chocolate factory to five sweepstakes-winning children. Wonka is a zany eccentric who seems to grow rare and exotic chocolate plants that produce fully manufactured candy. One of the first stops on the factory tour is a stroll through his candy garden, and the contest winners are allowed to feast on all the unusual edible flora their stomachs can handle. This sequence alone makes "Willy Wonka" one of the best food movies of all time.

Running through the middle of the garden is Wonka's chocolate river. He explains that a river is the best way to keep chocolate mixed, and it is the one thing that is verboten to touch. It should be noted that the chocolate river, from a production standpoint, looks more like mud or sewage than chocolate. It's watery and unappealing. Augustus, however, cannot help spooning some of the chocolate river into his mouth. He then slips and falls into the water, splashing around for a bit before being sucked into a drainage pipe.

According to Polygon's 2021 oral history of this scene, that river was as gross in person as it looked on camera. Böllner recalled having to film this moment for a long stretch, forcing him to repeatedly fall into, in his words, "stinky water." Also, it was cold. So, much less fun that actually swimming in liquid chocolate.

Michael Böllner added that he had to fall into a deep aperture under the water every time he dove into the river. The aperture, however, wasn't very large, and he repeatedly risked slamming his head into the solid river floor. As he put it:

"It was actually not chocolate. It was terribly cold. It was stinky water! And it was all day long, jumping in and jumping out, and being around with wet clothes. [...] The river was just 10 centimeters deep. And there was a hole about a square meter that I had to hit. So, I was very scared that I would not hit the square meter and would punch my head in the ground of the chocolate river."

Böllner didn't say what, exactly, the river smelled like, but its brackish, near-translucent brown might make one suspect that it was colored with paint. Julie Dawn Cole, who played the spoiled Veruca Salt in "Willy Wonka," also recalled poor Böllner's experience falling into that river all day. According to her, the water was not the least bit fresh, remaining stagnant for weeks. What's more, it seems that the film's cast and/or crew kept using it as a means of disposing of their drinks (which may very well explain the odor):

"Michael had to fall into this disgusting stuff that had been sitting there for three weeks. It had the lights on it, and people were emptying their coffee cup dregs into it."

So, Böllner had to splash into an unseen trough covered by three-week-old brown coffee water. Movie magic!

At the end of the chocolate river scene, Augustus, as mentioned, is sucked up a transparent pipe. His body blocks the pipe, though, and one can see his screaming face through the glass while chocolate pressure builds up beneath him. To film this moment, Michael Böllner had to be lowered into a tube, about six feet long in actuality, that was then filled with chocolate water. Naturally, Böllner did not enjoy this, either, explaining:

"It was a really tough thing because they took about two meters tube around me and filled it up with water up to my mouth. So, I couldn't move anything. I couldn't do anything. I just had to rely on the guys that were around me that don't drop me."

Peter Ostrum, who played Charlie Bucket, the protagonist of "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," also commented on the whole river scene, recalling that it looked utterly miserable. He knew the water was cold and gross, so he was merely relieved he didn't have to do the stunt himself. To quote him directly:

"When I saw Michael do take after take after take of falling in the cold river, that cold, dirty river, I just thought, 'I'm glad that's him and not me!'"

Indeed, this scene is but one of many reasons why folks of a certain age remember "Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory" as being delightful nightmare fuel. That and Willy Wonka is quite the twisted trickster in the film (something you can partly thank Gene Wilder himself for). As for its young stars, they all largely went on to enjoy various careers outside of acting. Luckily, none of them ever had to deal with brackish fake rivers again.

#3520. Could ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Re-Ignite Quentin Tarantino’s Bruce Lee Controversy?

It does not take long for the new trailer for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” to invoke the most discourse-inducing scene from “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” In fact, the very first words we hear are “You heard the story about Bruce Lee getting his ass kicked by a stuntman?” Another reference to the Bruce Lee scene follows soon after, long before we hear any mention of Rick Dalton or any of the more consequential events of the first film..

The Netflix pseudo-sequel, directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino, sees Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role as Cliff Booth. It’s billed as a separate adventure that happens to feature one of the film’s main characters — Leonardo DiCaprio is either completely absent or an incredibly well-kept secret, and Tarantino has said the film shares more DNA with Elmore Leonard’s paperback crime novels than the hangout movie style that defined the first film. But the marketing had to remind audiences who Cliff Booth is, and it’s curious that the second trailer’s primary reference point is a scene that is more memorable for the controversies it sparked than its role in the film’s plot. No mention is made, for instance, of the part Cliff played in dispatching several members of the Manson Family. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

A brief recap for those lucky enough to have been offline during the original saga. “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” features a scene in which Cliff is left to hang around a TV set while DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton shoots an episode. While killing time, he ends up in a fight with Bruce Lee (played by Mike Moh). Neither man is particularly polite to the other, with Cliff appearing more interested in Lee’s sidekick role on “The Green Hornet” than his higher profile movie roles, and Lee quickly challenges him to a fight. Each man wins one round of the fight before it’s broken up, ensuring there’s no clear winner — but the mere fact that Cliff was able to throw a martial arts legend into the side of a car is a feather in his cap.

Following the film’s release, Bruce Lee’s daughter Shannon publicly objected to the way the film portrayed her father.

“It’s unfortunate because it has started this narrative in some places where some people are saying, ‘Oh, Bruce Lee was an asshole,’” Shannon Lee said in 2020. “Look, everybody can be an asshole sometimes. I can be arrogant and angry in my life — is that something I would say I am like generally? No, my father was not generally like that. He was extremely passionate and driven.”

She continued, “He could have a temper sometimes, but he did not go around challenging people to fights. Certainly not after he was a teenager. Anyway, he didn’t behave or boast in that way…My father worked extremely hard and directly toward the idea of authentic representation in Hollywood for an Asian man, so I don’t think he would’ve gone around beating up stunt people and that kind of stuff as a way of furthering his cause.”

Tarantino frequently defended the scene, saying that he based his fictional portrayal on real anecdotes about Lee from people who knew the actor.

“Bruce Lee was kind of an arrogant guy,” Tarantino said in a 2019 press conference. “The way he was talking, I didn’t just make a lot of that up. I heard him say things like that to that effect. If people are saying, ‘Well he never said he could beat up Mohammad Ali,’ well yeah he did. Alright? Not only did he say that but his wife, Linda Lee, said that in her first biography I ever read. She absolutely said that.”

The controversy still rears its head sporadically. During a 2021 appearance on “The Joe Rogan Experience,” Tarantino told critics of the scene to “suck a dick,” with the caveat that he understood why a daughter would object to any negative portrayal of her father.

By the time “The Futher Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” hits select theaters this month (and expands to Netflix in December), more than seven years will have passed since “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” premiered. Perhaps all parties have said everything there is to say about the Bruce Lee scene. But given how much the trailer leans into the matter, we could be in for another round of arguments about the portrayal.

#3519. 39 Years Later, Inigo Montoya's Princess Bride Line Is Still The Greatest Movie Quote Ever

Do you love big, sweeping, epic romances where the lovers are kept apart for years, only to reunite in a scene that takes your breath away? Do you love clever, quippy, dialogue? Do you love swashbuckling adventures with a touch of vengeance? Great news. "The Princess Bride" has literally all of those things.

In 1987, writer-director Rob Reiner released "The Princess Bride," an adaptation of William Goldman's novel of the same name — and with Goldman adapting his own work into the screenplay, every second isn't just true to the book, but elevates the material. Robin Wright made her feature film debut as Princess Buttercup, a lovelorn woman who mourns the apparent loss of her one true love, a stable boy named Westley (Cary Elwes), and, believing him dead, agrees to marry the horrible Prince Humperdinck (Chris Sarandon). Elsewhere, swordsman Inigo Montoya (Mandy Patinkin), who always travels with the friendly giant Fezzik (André the Giant), wants revenge on the man who killed his father, and when Westley reappears as the Dread Pirate Roberts, he ends up teaming up with Inigo and Fezzik to also rescue Buttercup. Wallace Shawn, Carol Kane, and Billy Crystal play pivotal supporting roles in this film. It's basically perfect.

If you've seen "The Princess Bride" — and the odds are that you have — you know it's chock-a-block full of quotable lines. Today, though, we're celebrating one of its most beloved and well-known quotes, 39 years after its release.

Throughout "The Princess Bride," Mandy Patinkin's dashing and skilled swordsman Inigo Montoya has one goal: to find the six-fingered man who killed his father when Inigo was just a boy. For years, Inigo has been searching for this specific killer to avenge his dear old dad — and he finds him in the film in the form of Count Tyrone Rugen (Christopher Guest). So why is this line so important to the film, and why is it so beloved after nearly four decades?

For one thing, Inigo says it, like, 80 times in the movie, so it's easy to remember. It's a testament to Rob Reiner's sharp, exacting sense of comedic timing that the line never loses any luster, but remains funny every single time Patinkin delivers it (which is also a credit to Patinkin, a truly formidable performer who's been excellent for generations at this point). It's also connected to the movie's enduring message of love, even though it definitely seems a little more murdery than the flowery declarations of passion exchanged between Westley and Buttercup. Inigo truly loved his father, and once he kills the genuinely evil Rugen, the character delivers a line that defined Patinkin's actual life.

Reiner, who was tragically killed alongside his wife Michele Singer Reiner in late 2025 at his home in Los Angeles, made movies with big jokes and even bigger hearts. This line perfectly exemplifies that, and across the board, "The Princess Bride" is one of his very best films. So what other "Princess Bride" quotes stand the test of time?

#3517. VisionQuest Is Great, But Disney's Similar Sci-Fi Fantasy Series From 5 Years Ago Is Still Superior

As expected, VisionQuest is a creative, clever, and intriguing new entry in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, though it still can't quite live up to its genre-bending predecessor. Starring returning MCU favorites Paul Bettany and James Spader as Vision and Ultron, respectively, VisionQuest concludes a superhero journey that began in the much-maligned yet no less impactful Avengers: Age of Ultron, examining what it means to feel, love, and be human. Bettany and Spader are both excellent, and the show is especially appealing to die-hard MCU fans, a substantial reward for a decade of franchise loyalty.

Visually, many of VisionQuest's scenes are stunning, especially when Ultron and fellow familiar MCU AIs like F.R.I.D.A.Y., J.A.R.V.I.S., DUM-E, U, and Spider-Man: Far From Home's E.D.I.T.H. spend their time rooting around in Vision's Sherlockian, 1960s-inspired Mind Palace, digging deep into his hard drive to help this new and not-quite-improved version of Vision understand and accept his identity. He has the original Vision's memories, but only because Wanda Maximoff recreated him in her hex. What does that make White Vision? And how does that impact his relationship with Tommy Maximoff, Wanda and Westview-Vision's conjured son? It's a lot to wrap one's mind around.

While there's so much to like, and the show has set up an exciting finale, VisionQuest also suffers, at times, from a lack of focus. It ping-pongs between Vision's increasingly chaotic mind, his father-son bonding time with Tommy, Paladin's contract, Ultron's shady desires, and a new synthezoid's homicidal killing spree. It forgets what made Marvel's first Disney+ show so effective. Despite all the magical sitcom hijinks and SWORD's desperation to break into Westview, WandaVision's story always revolved around one specific, relatable, emotional theme.

Even now, five years and well over a dozen shows later, WandaVision remains one of the MCU's most impressive TV achievements, a surprising but highly effective blend of psychological, character-driven storytelling and a fantastical, mysterious superhero plot. Though WandaVision also had multiple storylines, including flashbacks to Wanda's life after Avengers: Endgame and SWORD's operation to break the Westview Hex, everything referenced or directly impacted Wanda's overwhelming grief and her hopeless desire to uphold her newly imagined life.

Vision, Tommy, Billy, Agatha Harkness, and even Monica Rambeau were all supporting players in her story. It never lost its focus. The same isn't true for VisionQuest. Ultron's, Tommy's, and Jocasta's needs and wants are all just as important as Vision's in the story's overall narrative arc. Add characters like Phineas Horton and JIM (both played brilliantly by Bettany), Tommy's friend Lisa, and multiple personified AIs, and it feels more like an ensemble drama than a character study.

As the penultimate episode of the series, VisionQuest episode 7 features a very exciting collection of Easter eggs, references, and key MCU ties.

There's nothing inherently wrong with that, of course — WandaVision's first "unofficial" sequel, Agatha All Along, was also an ensemble show, though that choice felt more purposeful. Agatha needed those characters to achieve her goals, and since their story was always bound together, the series never lost sight of its base narrative. Does Vision's journey to accept his existence and his innate ability to feel need all those moving parts? It's hard to say.

Both WandaVision and Agatha All Along also had a more cohesive creative "vision," as it were. Wanda's fascination with sitcoms served an undeniable purpose, as did the genre-mixing Witches' Road trials in Agatha All Along. They provided a structural framework. Between Vision's mental mansion, Jocasta's white void, London, and Madripoor, VisionQuest sometimes feels like watching multiple shows simultaneously, playing into well-worn superhero tropes. VisionQuest's version of the Hex and the Witches' Road is the digital mansion, but the story too often pivots in a new direction.

That said, VisionQuest is still a genuinely compelling story, a worthy end to the Marvel Cinematic Universe's unofficial Scarlet Witch trilogy. It's certainly leagues better than some of the MCU's other rushed shows, including Secret Invasion and She-Hulk: Attorney at Law. Like WandaVision and Agatha All Along, it explores universal themes like love, grief, identity, and parenthood with emotional finesse, all while experimenting with new kinds of storytelling. If this is where Vision's story ends — Bettany has not (yet) been confirmed for Avengers: Doomsday — then it's an undeniably effective and honorable sendoff.

All three series showcase how inventive superhero stories can be. Marvel doesn't need to be boxed in. It can explore different genres and structures, telling smaller, character-driven stories while still pushing the wider franchise forward. Like one of the MCU's other best trilogies, James Gunn's Guardians of the Galaxy, this is the story of the Maximoff family: a family made real and held together by love and heartache. There's nothing more human than that. The best superhero stories make these otherworldly, overpowered beings feel relatable and flawed. That's exactly what VisionQuest and the rest of Marvel's Scarlet Witch trilogy do too.

VisionQuest's finale releases Tuesday, November 10 on Disney+.

#3516. ‘Soul Patrol’ Review: The Vietnam War’s First Black Special Ops Team Shares Their Stories in An Enlightening Documentary

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. “Soul Patrol” opens in select theaters from Kino Lorber starting Friday, November 6.

The Vietnam War ended over a half-century ago, but the 20-year war remains a conflict that American artists keep going back to, finding new avenues and perspectives to tackle the many stories of the generation of men who had their lives irrevocably shaped by the conflict. Recent takes have centered the (often-neglected) perspective of the Vietnamese, or — like Spike Lee’s underrated late-career great “Da 5 Bloods” — explored the relatively under-examined service of Black men who served in the war. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“Soul Patrol,” a new documentary from director J.M. Harper, looks at the Black soldiers of the war through the perspective of Ed Emanuel, a writer who served as a 17-year-old. In his 2003 memoir of the same title, Emanuel described tracking down and reuniting with the men he served with in the first Black special operations Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol team, during his short 1968 to 1969 tour.

“Soul Patrol” finds the men in 2024, in what will be the last reunion they hold. Gathering together, the men — Emanuel, Lawton Mackey, Thad Givens, Emerson Branch, Jesse Lewis, Willie T. Brown, Willie Merkerson, and Norman Reid — sit in the conference room of a Florida hotel to discuss the memories of their service that has stuck with them over the decades, in the hope that their discussion can help them move on.

The opening, and Emmanuel’s narration, help bring context to the small stretch of the war that the film explores. In 1968, as the young men went to serve their country, America itself proved more turbulent than ever; Emanuel was on the plane to Vietnam as Robert F. Kennedy’s assassination was first reported. Protests against the war were growing, and the Civil Rights movement opposed the war as well; a speech from Martin Luther King Jr. becomes a crucial emotional turning point for Emanuel later, as he begins to wonder whether the trauma he experienced serving in the war was worth it.

Through the film, Emanuel and the footage of the reunion between the men guide the audience through their experiences, from the trauma they endured to the discrimination and tokenization they faced as Black soldiers fighting for America. One scene peels back at the men’s conflicting feelings around the nickname for their unit, a racialized moniker that’s simultaneously endearing and patronizing. Others focus on formative experiences Emanuel experiences throughout the war, including a hazy night in Bangkok that’s proves formative both sexually and emotionally.

Harper — whose debut feature “As We Speak” also played at Sundance — has a loud, uncompromisingly blunt style, and the film missteps most clearly when his directorial choices verge on heavy-handed. The film makes clumsy use of actor-led reenactments that are a little too slick and generic to slot seamlessly into the Super 8 footage and actor interviews that make up the bulk of the story. This particularly applies to an opening visual metaphor, in which an old veteran is haunted by a vision of his past, which proves more excessive and obvious than enlightening. Other formal choices feel designed to provoke emotional reactions the material can easily do on its own, particularly a loud, string-heavy score that feels overly generic for the material.

It’s when the film mostly gets out of its own way and lets the men’s experiences do the work that “Soul Patrol” really shines. The Super 8 footage collected from their tour in Vietnam, most of which was shot by the men themselves, is visually arresting and intimate, and Harper frequently employs quick cuts and montages of that on-the-ground film and b-roll of newscasts and ads of the time to flesh out the world they once inhabited. The reunion scenes are simply but artfully shot in black and white, including a revealing conversation among the men’s wives and partners about living with them that gently broadens the perspectives in the film’s portrait.

“Soul Patrol” admirably never tries to sum up the full experience of what Vietnam was, rather just trying to sum up what it was for these men. In the film’s closing stretch, it turns its attention to the men’s difficult experiences returning home from the war, with a candor and a vulnerability that’s hard not to tear up from. As one member of Soul Patrol reflects eloquently towards the end of the film, “We need to tell the stories to look at where we were at, where we come from, and where we headed. You need to know your beginning before you can figure out your ending.”

“Soul Patrol” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Kino Lorber opens the film in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3515. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

#3513. ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

For one of the most important screenings of “To Hold a Mountain,” the filmmakers had to bring their own electricity. In July, co-directors Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić hauled a tent, a generator, and a DCP up to the Montenegrin highlands where they had spent years filming.

The creative couple, also partnered in life, wanted the shepherds who lived and worked in Sinjajevina to see the movie they had made possible. But by then, Montenegro had already resolved their story’s central conflict — scrapping the government’s plan to turn these people’s ancestral pastures into a military training ground after joining NATO in 2017. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“To Hold a Mountain” won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize for documentary at Sundance, and Montenegro’s prime minister and president even showed up to the shepherds’ screening with their families, unannounced. When the film opens at New York’s Film Forum on December 16, American audiences will see the feature’s updated conclusion.

“We reopened the film to continue shooting and then a second end happened that was very empowering and powerful,” Tutorov said at IndieWire’s Art of the Doc series.

During our conversation, the filmmaker recalled arriving in Sinjajevina with Glomazić on the first day of protest. They wanted to help the community and make a movie, and agreed early on that those were two different jobs.

“We will separate our activist mission from our filmmaker’s mission,” she said. “That was a very good decision because it allowed us to be very bold in both roles.”

Onscreen, the fight over who would get to lay claim to the mountain centered on two people who already did: Gara, a shepherd and community leader, and Nada, the young girl she was raising. As the threat to their home brought a history of violence in their own family to the surface, the directors had to reckon with how much of Nada’s private life might become public.

“We really wanted it to be an empowering experience for [her],” Tutorov said.

Nada was twelve and a half when the filmmakers began to understand what the story would ask of her, and Tutorov said they decided to keep filming until she turned eighteen — precisely so Nada could decide for herself whether she wanted to be part of it. The crew logged more than 230 shooting days, though some yielded only half an hour of footage.

Gara and Nada had work to do, too. The directors and cinematographer Eva Kraljević shared a small shepherd’s shed, assisting with various chores including cows that had to be milked twice a day. Over successive summers, their routine became a framing device. Tutorov, who studied art history, thinks of the mountain as a kind of chorus bearing witness to living things on it.

Last July, just as the filmmakers were wrapping up, Montenegro’s government canceled the training-ground plan. Tutorov believes “To Hold a Mountain” and how it told the existing community’s story influenced that decision. She also pointed out that a different government was in power by 2025, following years of organizing by Sinjajevina locals.

At the shepherd’s screening a year later, Prime Minister Milojko Spajić said the film reinforced his view that canceling the plan had been the right call. Then Montenegro chose “To Hold a Mountain” as its official submission for the international feature Oscar. Tutorov said there was irony in realizing that, after years of fighting the government, she and Glomazić would be proudly representing the country on a global stage.

“It feels like they really kind of destroyed our strategy,” she said, warmly.

It’s a good joke, and an even better reason to remember that rough-and-tumble showing. For an evening, the people who’d spent years making their case to the government got to host its leaders on the very land they’d fought to keep. Tutorov recalled what Montenegro’s president told the filmmakers after seeing the movie: “Thank you guys for teaching us democracy.”

#3510. Dungeon Crawler Carl Book 9 Release Date Is Sooner Than You Think

Dungeon Crawler Carl readers may be among the luckiest fanbase in terms of the sheer amount of content available in the series and how quickly it was released since the first book. To put things into perspective, the first Dungeon Crawler Carl novel was self-published in October 2020, and by May 2026, the eighth installment, A Parade of Horribles, had already arrived. That's eight substantial novels in less than six years, a publishing pace that puts some of fantasy's biggest franchises to shame.

George R.R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire, for example, has just five main novels since A Game of Thrones debuted in 1996, with readers still waiting for The Winds of Winter more than 15 years after the last book. Even Rebecca Yarros' enormously popular Fourth Wing series, which began in 2023, has only seen three main installments. Dinniman, meanwhile, has kept Carl and Donut's story moving at an extraordinary pace, and he's already released teaser chapters for Book 9 to boot.

All that is to say that, despite not having a specific release window for Book 9, currently titled The Beautiful Place, Dungeon Crawler Carl fans are likely to see it sooner rather than later.

Looking at Matt Dinniman's publication history, the pace of Dungeon Crawler Carl has been remarkable, although the gaps between books have gradually grown longer, which is expected considering the books are also getting longer. The first novel debuted in 2020, followed by Carl's Doomsday Scenario in January 2021, The Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook in April, and The Gate of the Feral Gods in July. That amounts to four substantial novels released in less than a year, which is honestly wild.

Book 5, The Butcher's Masquerade, dropped in February 2022, but from there, the gaps started to grow a bit as the narrative started to get a bit more complicated. Readers waited roughly 16 months for The Eye of the Bedlam Bride, which released in July 2023, and another 16 months for This Inevitable Ruin in November 2024. Finally, there was roughly another 18-month wait for A Parade of Horribles, which just launched earlier this year in May.

Fortunately, Dinniman has offered some insight into when readers might expect Book 9. In a July 2026 interview with West Sound Magazine, the author confirmed that work was underway and estimated a similar turnaround, saying, "About a year, give or take a few months." At San Diego Comic-Con that same month, he also suggested that finishing Book 9 and a substantial portion of Book 10 would take approximately another year.

However, there's an important complication with these final installments. Dinniman has confirmed that he's effectively writing one enormous conclusion that will be published across two books. In an October interview with Collider, he described the process as "easily the most difficult thing I've ever written," suggesting the finale could require additional time.

Based on the recent more-lengthy gaps between installments, late 2027 seems like a reasonable prediction for Book 9, although an early 2028 release certainly wouldn't be surprising. Dinniman has already shared the prologue, Chapters 1–5, and an interlude with Patreon supporters, confirming substantial work is underway. For now, though, the book remains without an official release date.

Based on the content in those teaser chapters, Dinniman is off to a strong start with Book 9, even if it's only a short taste of the larger release. If you are all caught up on Dungeon Crawler Carl and aren't already part of Dinniman's Patreon page, it's well worth joining, and you can get a look at the preview teaser chapters for a few bucks a month. Further, you'll get a look at any other preview content ahead of the actual book release, and updates on what's going on in the author's life as well.

Overall, Dinniman's publishing history and projections for Dungeon Crawler Carl Book 9's release are all incredibly promising indications that we're likely to see The Beautiful Place sooner rather than later.
