#3483. 7 Apple TV Sci-Fi Shows With No Bad Seasons, Ranked

Apple TV is quickly carving a space for itself as one of the best streamers for sci-fi TV shows. These series run the gamut from cerebral and mind-binding to apocalyptic, even comedic. If you're looking for a good sci-fi show, Apple TV has you covered. There's even a long forgotten hidden gem series that is unlike any other you've ever seen on television.

With many of these shows still going, set to debut new seasons within the year, it's the perfect time to catch up or re-watch so you're ready for the continuation of the story. They not only count among the best sci-fi series on Apple TV, but the best sci-fi series of the last five years, period.

A seriously mind-bending show, Dark Matter stars Joel Edgerton as Jason Dessen, a physicist and college professor who is abducted by an alternate version of himself known as Jason2 and taken to another reality. If Jason doesn't get back to his reality, Jason2 threatens to infiltrate his life and take up with his family, posing as the real Jason.

With a fantastic cast that also includes Jennifer Connelly, Alice Braga, and Jimmi Simpson, Dark Matter is a near-perfect hard sci-fi show with two seasons under its belt so far, the second season wrapping up at the end of October 2026. There's no official renewal yet for a third season, but the story was originally planned as a three-season arc, so it would be surprisingly if Apple TV prematurely pulled the plug. This is all the more reason to watch seasons one and two and be ready for the likely end to the story. The series, based on the Blake Crouch novel, uses sci-fi to pose existential questions about humanity, living with your choices, and the concept of exploring the road not taken to determine if fate is defined, and what is the sum of one's choices.

Alexander Skarsgård is brilliant in the sci-fi action comedy Murderbot as the title character, a private security construct who has managed to hack its own governor module and become sentient. But this is a dangerous position to be in, because if anyone finds out, Murderbot will be destroyed. So, it does its best to pretend it's simply a robot there to obey demands with no awareness beyond that. But that's easier said than done because humans are downright weird. Murderbot gets assigned to work with an eccentric team whose members begin to realize that something is off. Meanwhile, all Murderbot wants to do is binge-watch episodes of its favorite sci-fi show, stored in its own memory.

Murderbot is a sweet and funny tale about fitting in, acceptance, and understanding human nature and emotions. The show explores topics of AI, sentient robots, and, at its core, human weakness, human nature, and autonomous thinking. Unlike more serious sci-fi shows, you'll get plenty of laughs as this powerful robot displays very relatable, socially awkward traits housed in its human-like body. Alongside Skarsgård, the talented cast is led by Noma Dumezweni, a standout as team leader Ayda Mensah, and David Dastmalchian as Gurathin, a construct/human hybrid and tech expert who prides himself (itself?) on being able to understand both worlds.

I had never seen anything like Calls on television before and still haven't since. The mystery thriller analog animated miniseries based on the French series of the same name isn't a show you watch like a traditional one. All that you see on screen are geometric shapes, moving lines, and text that appears and disappears, pulses, and scrolls as dialogue is being spoken. Every episode is a phone call between two or more people as they discuss strange happenings.

The narrative comes together in the end, but every episode feels like a standalone story before you start to piece things together. What makes Calls stand out even more is the incredible voice cast with dozens of names, including actors like Aubrey Plaza, Clancy Brown, Pedro Pascal, Nick Jonas, Rosario Dawson, and more. The stories are bizarre yet terrifying, from a woman reporting to her boyfriend that an entity that doesn't look human has entered her home, to another who receives a phone call from her while standing next to what appears to be her dead body. You will initially want to turn Calls off, thinking it isn't for you. But stick with it: it pays off, and you'll be deeply invested by the end of Episode 1.

The sci-fi drama For All Mankind takes you on a journey through alternate history. What if the global space race didn't end once the Soviet Union achieved the first Moon landing ahead of the U.S.? Set in 1969, Alexei Leonov is the first human to land on the Moon and NASA is deflated. It pushes forward with its research projects, matching the Soviet Union's decision to train female astronauts as well as ethnic minorities so it can keep up. The competition heats up throughout the story in the "what if" scenario, which will continue through to a sixth and final season in 2027.

Once you catch up on For All Mankind, one of the best sci-fi shows released since 2010, you can check out the equally great Star City. The spin-off focuses on the Soviet space program and has received rave reviews. That show premiered in May 2026, and though it has not yet been officially renewed for a second season, it's likely there will be one. But start with For All Mankind, one of Apple TV's first original series. It's a stunning visual show with a narrative that spans decades, fantastic performances, and a plot that dives as much into the human side of the story as the alternate historical space race one.

Sure, it's easy to deliver a show with no bad seasons when the series only has one season so far. But it's safe to assume that when Pluribus returns for its confirmed second season, it will likely be just as fantastic as Season 1. Hailing from the warped mind of Vince Gilligan, the post-apocalyptic sci-fi show tells the story of an alien virus that takes over Earth. Yes, people die. But many survive. There's just one problem: they are now unwittingly part of a hive mind, connected with shared knowledge, memories, resources, and a goal. They seemingly want to create a utopian society where everyone lives in peace and harmony.

Carol Sturka (Rhea Seehorn) survives, but she's one of a baker's dozen of humans from around the world who are immune. With all its vast knowledge, the hive mind can't yet figure out why and is working furiously on a way to have these 13 people "join us." The story explores the importance of individuality and power over your own life. It forces you to ask questions about whether a perfect society is even achievable. The cycle of life suggests that for some to survive, others can't. Watching will make you rethink the idea of world peace if it comes at a cost of personal agency.

One of the most gripping sci-fi series of the last five years, Silo is set to end its four-season arc in July 2027. So, you have plenty of time to catch up on the three seasons to date. The sci-fi dystopian drama is set in a far future when civilization has existed in underground silos for centuries. A catastrophic event obliterated Earth above and everyone lives with the supposed knowledge that it's not safe to go outside. Doing so will result in immediate death. Juliette Nichols (Rebecca Ferguson) is a razor-sharp engineer caught up in a tragedy when her boyfriend winds up dead, and murder is suspected. As she follows clues given to her by others, she discovers that not everything is what it seems.

Silo doesn't dive fully into the sci-fi angle until Season 3, but the set-up through the first two seasons is worth the wait. The story and characters are compelling. The way the silo operates on a class-based system leaves you wondering if recreating society would only lead to us making the same mistakes all over again. Based on the Hugh Howey novels, which count among the greatest dystopian book trilogies of all time, Silo diverts from the novel narrative just enough such that even if you're already familiar with the story, you'll find the show equally compelling but different enough to keep you guessing.

A show arguably hasn't been dissected and analyzed so much since Lost. In the 10/10 masterpiece dystopian sci-fi show Severance, Mark Scout (Adam Scott) undergoes an experimental procedure to sever his memories. His "innie" persona goes to work every day sitting at a computer doing a mundane and repetitive task he doesn't even understand. At home, his "outie" is unaware of what he has done all day but is happy for the reprieve from grieving the loss of his wife. As these two versions of the same person start to intersect, Mark becomes aware of things he shouldn't, and he and his team members start to question the nature of their realities and who they really are.

The sci-fi psychological thriller is bizarre, yet captivating, and one of the most visually stunning shows on television right now, arguably ever. Elements of the story will rack your brain. You'll become emotionally invested in every character. Yes, even those who are sort of two different people inside and outside the office. It's a workplace show like no other that explores the topics of human emotion, dealing with grief, and playing with identity.

#3482. Developers can now create advanced ‘app skills’ for Siri AI

Apple today announced a major new Siri AI initiative for third-party developers, allowing any app to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. The first versions of Siri AI were limited to a much smaller set of supported schemas.

The new ‘app skills’ also let apps teach Siri how to coordinate complicated multi-step actions. These features are testable in the iOS 27.3 betas.

The app skills sound very similar to what other LLM-driven AI models offer, enabling richer understanding of complicated tasks.

For example, a flight tracking app skill will be able to cleanly map what app intents Siri should use to service a particular kind of user request; something that the first version of Siri AI was simply incapable of doing.

Of course, Apple itself has also taken advantage of the new Siri AI foundational features, with a significant rollout of new capabilities across Apple’s apps.

Here’s an example of what Siri will be able to do, from the developer documentation:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

It’s also going to be a lot easier to initiate Siri actions for third-party apps. With the Siri AI Developer Preview, users don’t have to explicitly mention the app’s name in many circumstances. For instance, if a Live Activity for a ride-sharing app is active, Siri will automatically understand that a request to “change the ride address” corresponds to the app driving the Live activity.

This gives you a sense of the kinds of things Siri will be able to do in the future, coordinating more complicated actions across Apple and third-party apps.

The new OS releases are in developer beta right now, but Apple says the app skills support is only an early developer preview and is scheduled to officially roll out in the spring.

#3481. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3478. 6 Superhero Characters Who Work Best on TV

With how prevalent superheroes have become in movies and television over the decades, it's become more and more clear that some heroes work better in one medium over another. This isn't to say that because a hero works in one medium, they can't work in another, but there are some that simply thrive more in television or movies, respectively.

Television has proven to be a great outlet for superhero storytelling, thanks to how much time a character gets to spend with the audience. Whether it be because their world is simply best executed on a smaller television budget, they have more day-to-day storytelling, or benefit from spending more time with an audience than the average bear, superhero TV is sometimes the best medium for some heroes. These characters prove exactly why that can be.

While the Disney+ television era of the Marvel Cinematic Universe had its fair share of complaints, there are still some series that people liked, and one of them is, without a doubt, Moon Knight. While—thanks to his mythology and power set—one might initially think that he would actually fit better on the big screen, Marvel's white-clad superhero has already proven why he works better on television. When a character isn't massively known by general audiences, sometimes they actually benefit more from being a show because audiences get to spend more time with them and can grow more attached to them than they could in just two hours.

Over the course of Disney+'s Moon Knight, viewers got to spend almost six hours with Oscar Isaac's iconic hero, getting them attached to him better than they ever could have before. It's gotten to the point that people are begging to see him in other Marvel content now because of it. There's also a hefty dose of mystery and lore to uncover in the hero's mythological roots and the many unexplored corners of his mind, and the way it's covered over the many hours of the series couldn't have been done in a movie. It's actually pretty safe to say that Moon Knight would not have worked as well as a movie, making the character genuinely better-suited for television.

Sometimes a lot of it comes down to budget management, and that is most definitely the case with Green Arrow. Because of the character not having superpowers and being a bow and arrow-wielding hero, far less budget is necessary for bringing the Emerald Archer to life than others—even the likes of other non-powered heroes like Batman. While they could make a Green Arrow movie and do some cool stuff within it because of the less budget needed for the hero, executing his stories on television ends up being the better move, with no question.

He's already been a success on TV, actually, via the CW's Arrow (despite being more of a Batman show than a Green Arrow show). Why use the extra budget leftover from not needing to execute superpowers for a 2-hour story, when one could use that extra budget across an entire season of a show? This would allow the studios to do more on a week-to-week basis, rather than a one-time go in theaters. Not to mention, the hero's stories aren't usually gigantic world-ending threats that require the kind of budget a typical superhero movie has. Again, it becomes a case of being able to simply do more on television than they could in a film.

If it isn't already obvious, the one and only Invincible (Steven Yeun) has quickly become one of the most prominent television superheroes of all time. The show is already adapting the book very accurately, and people are adoring it. So . . . why is there a movie in development? This is a question that has rested on the minds of fans for quite some time, because everyone can agree that the show is pretty much the best medium for the series.

Invincible is already adapting the entire comic book run—so long as they go for the amount of seasons they want to—so the concept of doing him in a movie feels a bit redundant. There's simply no question that Invincible is already the best of what an adaptation of the series could be, so it warrants the title of this character working best on television. Why even try to fix something that's not broken?

This character has already starred in an animated television show—Static Shock—and it was exceptional. This is primarily because the protagonist, Virgil Hawkins (Phil LaMarr), is a very grounded, street-level hero. He's just a 16-year-old kid who's trying to do his best—a Spider-Man-esque character, in a way. Coming-of-age stories are great, and there are plenty of coming-of-age movies, but this genre on television can often be far more effective.

Getting to spend a decent amount of time with a character who's growing so much into the person they're going to be—like Virgil is, on a superpowered scale—allows the audience to really gravitate towards and fall in love with the protagonist. It also gives viewers time to really explore the hero's world and dive into the characters that surround him, fleshing out his journey into a whole new depth.

Four people, four completely different ideas of what it means to have somebody in your corner. Here is who picked up, what they would ask of you, and what you would get back.

You want the friend who does not leave. Steve is the one who turns up at the door without being asked, who remembers what you said you were worried about, and who has never once made you audition for his attention.

You want the friend who is genuinely exhausting and completely worth it. Tony will forget your birthday, then build you something at four in the morning that you did not know you needed, and hand it over as though it were nothing.

You want the friend who replies in four seconds and apologises for it. Peter is earnest in a way that is almost unfashionable, and he will take on far more than he can carry rather than admit that he is struggling.

You want the friend who insults your shoes, fixes your phone and then quietly rearranges your entire life for the better. Shuri does not do soft reassurance, and that is the reason you would believe her when she says you are fine.

One of the most famous and beloved Marvel television shows is the one and only Daredevil—no contest. The televised story of Matt Murdock (Charlie Cox) has become so popular that people begged for the show and the actor to return, leading to the announcement of the sequel series, Daredevil: Born Again. The Netflix series is genuinely considered a true work of art.

This character is much like a lot of other television-preferred superheroes in the fact that he is a street-level hero, and far more grounded than others. This makes it far easier to depict him on television, and having the extra time for viewers to watch him makes the political thriller and mystery aspects of the show have so much more time to be more complex than they ever could have been in just a movie.

Despite Spider-Man: Brand New Day being within the top three highest-grossing movies of all time, the character of Spider-Man is easily better suited for television. The best parts about the character are the coming-of-age aspects of his journey, his gigantic group of supporting characters, and even larger catalog of villains. Sure, these things are adapted very well to film—the large number of massively successful films being prooof—but his stories told on television can often be considered some of the best adaptations of the character, period.

A great example of this is the likes of The Spectacular Spider-Man—a series that has episodes that can genuinely be considered masterpieces—and Spider-Man: The Animated Series. These are noted by many to be some of the best iterations of the character ever put onto screen, and that's not for no reason. The huge amount of time audiences have spent with these versions of the character makes for a connection unlike any other. Not to mention, the fact that they're animated means they have no restrictions when it comes to bringing certain characters to life—limitless potential for comic accurate designs and unique powers—and allows for some amazing spectacle.

Is this the best implementation of touchscreen controls on a laptop?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Apple has long opposed releasing a touchscreen MacBook, with Steve Jobs himself calling touchscreen laptops “ergonomically terrible” and saying that “touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical.” As recently as 2021, current Apple CEO John Ternus stated that “the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input” and that Apple hadn’t “felt a reason to change that."

Now, in late 2026, Apple has reversed course by releasing the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display — its very first touchscreen MacBook.

Touchscreen laptops have been around for almost two decades, so Apple is decidedly late to the party here. That said, the wait has arguably been worth it for touchscreen lovers, as the feature works as well as Apple has advertised. As someone who has tested dozens of touchscreen laptops, I can tell you that the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is easily among the best.

In my MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review, I discussed the laptop’s touch functionality. However, I want to go into more detail here, as the touchscreen experience has been more useful than I expected. I won’t say it’s converted me into a touchscreen laptop enthusiast, but it has certainly made a strong case for a feature I’ve typically dismissed in the laptops I’ve reviewed.

Below, I’ll detail how the MacBook Pro OLED’s touchscreen works and what it’s like to use for everyday tasks. I’ll also cover some of the drawbacks, as this touch display isn’t without faults. With that said, let’s dive in.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display impresses thanks to its astonishing touchscreen OLED display that’s the brightest we’ve ever seen on a laptop. On top of that, it has a thinner, lighter design, punchy speakers, and super-long battery life. Plus. Apple finally ditches the notch. While it’s very expensive, this marvelous laptop will blow you away.

Most laptops like the Dell XPS 16 (2026) use a separate digitizer to support touch input. But with the PROLED, Apple built the touch sensor directly into the display panel rather than layering it on top. This reduces latency and delivers higher-precision touch controls. The display supports the common gestures you’re used to, such as swiping, pinch-to-zoom, drag-and-drop, and double-tapping.

In practice, the touchscreen feels snappy and intuitive. Again, I test a lot of touchscreen laptops, and I immediately noticed how much faster the MacBook Pro responds to touch than its competitors. Using the touchscreen feels more like interacting with an iPad. I didn't notice any input lag.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Though I initially had to consciously use touch controls because I’m so used to doing everything on the keyboard and touchpad, I eventually switched between both. For example, I’d open apps by clicking the touchpad and then use my fingers to rearrange them on the touchscreen. I especially like how the red, yellow, and green window dots get bigger when you hold your finger over them, which also brings up the window-tiling options.

I mostly use Google apps like Docs and Drive for work, and so far I haven’t run into any issues with touch controls. Apple says many third-party applications already take advantage of touch controls, but some might not work as well. So far, I haven’t encountered any.

Even though I test touchscreen laptops, I don’t often use touch controls. I always assumed it was because I could do anything I needed with keyboard shortcuts and the touchpad. But given how much I use touch controls on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, I wonder if I just didn’t like how (relatively) unintuitive the experience was on those Windows machines. Whatever the reason, I think it’s a small miracle that this laptop has made me use a feature I previously all but dismissed or ignored.

Touch controls work well on the OLED MacBook Pro, but they have some drawbacks.

First, the touchscreen doesn’t support the Apple Pencil Pro. This is especially baffling since Apple itself says you can draw on the screen. While you can technically draw with your finger, I don’t think most artists would want to. Not only would it be uncomfortable, but a stylus offers more versatility than your natural digits.

Speaking of comfort, I also can’t imagine musicians opting to play a virtual piano/keyboard on the touchscreen. Again, this is technically possible, but I imagine it would be murder on your back and shoulders if you do that for extended periods.

On a related note, I found it interesting that many folks on YouTube asked us whether the PROLED MacBook Pros are iPad replacements. I’m not sure where that idea came from, especially since the display doesn’t flip like a 2-in-1 convertible laptop. Sure, the touchscreen is as responsive as on an iPad, but the laptop’s form factor alone prevents it from being an iPad replacement. And again, without Apple Pencil support, you wouldn’t get a 1:1 iPad experience anyway.

Even if Apple was hesitant to introduce touch to MacBooks, I think it’s ultimately good that the company now gives customers the option. Yes, that option also comes with a steep price tag of $2,899 for the 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, but it’s there for folks who can genuinely use it—even with some of the inherent flaws I detailed above.

Now that touchscreen MacBooks are real, I wonder how much further Apple will push things. For instance, will the company eventually release 2-in-1 MacBooks that are better suited for iPad-like use? We can’t know for sure, but the door seems open now that Apple has reversed its stance on touchscreen laptops. Who knows what to expect?

While the touchscreen on the MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR Display lacks Apple Pencil support and can be awkward at times, it mostly works as advertised. That might change with more testing, and I’ll report on it if and when it happens. Right now, though, I’m going to consider the MacBook Pro touchscreen a success.

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with a surprisingly extensive set of new features and improvements across the system. One of them is the expansion of the iPhone Duo’s redesigned StandBy experience to other iPhone models. Here are the details.

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, one of its exclusive new features was a redesigned StandBy experience with new clock faces and expanded customization options.

StandBy mode was introduced with iOS 17, and it essentially turns the iPhone into a smart display when placed horizontally while charging.

Until now, users of other iPhone models were limited to the original StandBy experience, which offered clock, widget, and photo views, but lacked the additional faces and more extensive customization options introduced with the iPhone Duo.

With iOS 27.3, however, Apple is extending the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces to other iPhones, with additional options for customizing their colors and complications. In addition to the new Calendar and Weather faces, the update adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face, letting users choose which shared photos appear in StandBy.

Users with an iPhone 11 or later can now also create multiple versions of the same StandBy face, each with its own customization options, and swipe between them.

Baking soda can make a great weed killer — but only if you use it properly

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

No matter what time of year it is, there seems to be one gardening chore that feels like a never-ending challenge — weeds. This is especially the case in damp fall, when I’m finding my gravel paths and patio pavers littered with unsightly weeds.

And while larger, visible weeds with clear taproots are easy enough to pull out, pesky weeds stuck deep in narrow cracks and crevices are super tricky and time-consuming to remove.

Which is why I was thrilled to discover a kitchen staple that is the ultimate trick for clearing weeds between my pavers.

Baking soda has been a staple in my cleaning routine for years, and there are so many uses for this ingredient — but it can also be used as a homemade, cost-effective weed killer. This is due to its elevated sodium levels, which draw moisture out of plant cells, drying out young weeds. But how effective is this?

I asked gardening experts why baking soda actually kills weeds, and exactly how long it takes.

Similar to commercial weed killers, baking soda acts as a natural bioherbicide that kills weeds on direct contact with foliage. But how fast does it act?

"Visible damage may occur within about 24–48 hours, although results can vary depending on the size and type of weed, weather conditions, and how thoroughly the baking soda contacts the foliage," states Kathleen Hallal, VP of Landcare and Municipalities at FireHawk Bioherbicide.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

"Baking soda can be an effective household option for treating small weeds because its high sodium content can draw moisture from plant tissue and cause the weed to dry out."

"Visible damage may occur within about 24–48 hours, although results can vary depending on the size and type of weed"

Should you clear away the dead plants once the baking soda has done its job? "Once a weed has died, removing the dead plant material is generally a good idea, especially for appearance and to keep the area tidy," says Hallal.

While baking soda works well for eliminating smaller weeds, it cannot penetrate the deep taproot of larger varieties. To tackle larger weeds, you’ll need to pull them by hand or use dedicated tools and products.

Bear in mind, applying baking soda properly is vital —or else you risk causing unintended harm to your yard.

“When using this kind of method to kill weeds, it's important to be cautious and apply it carefully, as it may also damage surrounding plants and affect the soil if used repeatedly,” advises Paul Parker, plants and bulbs specialist at J. Parker’s.

“Once the weed has died back, it's best to remove it rather than leave it in place. Wait until the foliage has turned brown and withered, then carefully remove the plant using a small shovel and gloves. Try to remove as much of the root system as possible, particularly with perennial weeds, as any remaining roots may allow them to grow back.”

It’s also worth noting that using baking soda is only a temporary fix for young weeds. And for optimal results, it’s best to use it alongside other conventional weed-control techniques.

“Its main limitation is consistency,” adds Hallal. “Baking soda is not specifically formulated for weed control, so it can be difficult to get even coverage, and the powder can blow away or wash off in rain.”

Additionally, baking soda should be used sparingly, as it could have long-term effects on the quality of your soil. “Over time, excessive sodium can affect soil conditions and potentially harm desirable plants, so it should be used carefully around lawns, garden beds, and landscaped areas.”

However, baking soda is still great for occasional spot treatment for small weeds, particularly when tackling those pesky ones growing in paving cracks or driveways.

In any case, try this household staple the next time you need to banish small weeds - and it should take just 48 hours.

#3469. Netflix's One Piece Replaces Zoro As The Best Fighter In Season 3

One of the many great elements in Netflix's live-action One Piece adaptation so far has undoubtedly been the battle scenes. Incorporating wild Devil Fruit powers with sword fights and old-fashioned brawling, the Netflix series has landed on an action style that feels authentic to Eiichiro Oda's source material while still keeping one foot in the broadest realms of plausibility.

In One Piece's first season on Netflix, Monkey D. Luffy himself was granted the most impressive fight scene. The Straw Hat captain's final battle against Arlong proved to be a bone-crunching, fast-paced, and highly emotive clash that surpassed all bouts from episodes prior, thus cementing Luffy as One Piece's chief combatant.

Iñaki Godoy's character didn't see quite the same level of action in One Piece season 2, however. The big climax against Wapol resolved itself in relatively straightforward fashion, while Mr. 3 quickly fell to defeat once Luffy saw through his smoke and mirror antics.

Instead, it was Mackenyu's Roronoa Zoro who emerged from One Piece's second run looking like the show's best fighter. His epic deathmatch against the 100 Baroque Works agents at Whisky Peak added martial arts, acrobatics, and old-school stunt work to the show's usual brand of action, creating one of the most visually astounding sequences in any Netflix original series. With Luffy treading water against a hungry king and a talking candle, One Piece season 2 really was Zoro's time to shine.

But the pendulum is set to swing in Luffy's favor when One Piece season 3 drops in 2027. Adapting the Alabasta saga, every Straw Hat will get a featured battle if the TV series follows its source material. For his part, Zoro will go up against Baroque Works' Mr. 1, played in live-action by Awdo Awdo. Their meeting is guaranteed to be a blockbuster event that's almost but not quite as good as the rumble at Whisky Peak.

Just as no fight in One Piece season 2 could come close to matching Zoro vs. the 100 agents, no fight in season 3 is going to outshine Luffy vs. Crocodile. The violent encounter with Joe Manganiello's villain, who was introduced properly during the final moments of One Piece's season 2 finale, will be the pinnacle of the show so far, making Arlong look amateurish in comparison. It was great to see One Piece letting Luffy's first mate take center stage, but it's time for season 3 to remind everyone exactly why Luffy himself is the story's protagonist.

With every Straw Hat getting a big fight in One Piece's upcoming season, this will be the show's first opportunity to truly demonstrate where each character currently sits in terms of their power level.

Chopper looked fairly strong during his scenes in Drum Kingdom, but the same happened in the anime and manga, and it wasn't long after that he found himself tossed into the so-called 'weakling trio.' It remains to be seen whether the same will happen on Netflix.

Jacob Romero's Usopp has shown shrewd cunning and the ability to take plenty of punishment, completely in line with the character as Oda wrote him.

Nami has been afforded the biggest power-up in live-action, with Emily Rudd's version more capable in battle right from the start. That makes her season 3 date with Miss Doublefinger much more interesting, and their fight could end up being a surprise highlight of 2027's episodes.

Conversely, Sanji has drawn the shortest straw (hat) so far. Netflix's series has showcased his wit and charm, and even hinted at emotional depths that won't fully surface until sometime around season 10, but we haven't seen him kicking enemies into next week that often. One Piece season 3's Sanji vs. Mr. 2 matchup will be the perfect opportunity to change that.

#3468. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

Squeeze more out of your iPhone with these five clever, hidden problem-solvers

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every major iOS update brings a wave of headline features, but Apple has a habit of tucking some of its most practical tools away in obscure corners of the Settings app, or omitting them from your iPhone's main menus entirely.

Instead of novelty gimmicks you will try once and forget, these tucked-away toggles eliminate the daily friction points you thought you just had to live with. Here are five built-in iPhone features Apple buried beneath the surface, and how to turn each one on right now.

Sophisticated AI-cloned voices and spoofed messages make it increasingly difficult to spot social engineering scams targeting your personal data or finances. This on-device protection analyzes unusual communication patterns locally, without Apple reading your messages or emails, and alerts supported apps if high-risk fraud is suspected before you authorize a transfer or surrender credentials.

Taking phone calls in noisy environments often turns into a shouting match against street traffic, background chatter, or high winds. Voice Isolation uses machine learning to prioritize your vocal frequencies while aggressively filtering out surrounding racket. It lives outside the main Settings app and surfaces contextually while a call is underway.

To activate Voice Isolation, start or answer any cellular or FaceTime call. Swipe down from the top-right corner to open Control Center, tap Phone Controls (or Mic Mode), and select Voice Isolation.

Your iPhone includes a built-in signature tool tucked inside the native Markup suite that saves your signature permanently, allowing you to drop, resize, and place it on any document in seconds.

Open the document in Files or Photos (or take a screenshot of it), then tap the Markup pen icon. Tap the plus icon on the toolbar, select Signature, write your name once, and tap Done. All you need to do now is position and resize your saved signature over where you need to sign.

Lowering your daytime ringtone to avoid interrupting meetings used to create a real risk of sleeping straight through a silent alarm the next morning. iOS finally decouples these controls, allowing you to set a fixed wake-up volume that remains entirely untouched no matter how often you adjust your ringtone or alert slider.

Open Settings and tap Sounds & Haptics. Under Alarms & Timers, toggle Match Ringtone Volume to off. Then simply drag the dedicated slider to your preferred alarm level.

Night Shift changes display tones to warmer colors, but it does nothing to prevent the primary driver of digital eye strain: holding a screen inches away from your face for extended periods. Screen Distance uses the front TrueDepth camera to gauge proximity. If you hold your iPhone closer than 12 inches for several minutes, it temporarily pauses the display with a prompt to step back.

Simply open Settings, tap Screen Time, Screen Distance and toggle Screen Distance to on.

#3461. Apple now explicitly bans employees from using confidential information in prediction markets

Apple has updated its insider trading policy to explicitly prohibit employees from using confidential information to bet on prediction markets. Here are the details.

Following yesterday’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings report, Apple today published its fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, which is a mandatory annual filing with the SEC that provides a detailed look at the company’s finances, business, and risks.

Among the documents included in the filing is an updated version of Apple’s insider trading policy.

Until last year, Apple’s insider trading policy, filed with the SEC as Exhibit 19.1, included the following prohibitions:

However, the updated policy includes a new prohibition:

No Trading in Prediction Markets Based on Confidential Information. Do not participate in “prediction markets” or similar platforms to wager, bet, trade, buy or sell contracts based on the outcome of future events, or otherwise enter into event contracts, when such activity involves the use of Apple Confidential Information (as defined in Apple’s Business Conduct Policy) about Apple or any other company (including Apple suppliers, manufacturers, vendors or customers, such as cellular network carriers or other business partners) obtained in connection with your work at Apple. You must also not tip Apple Confidential Information to others who may participate in such markets. Apple Confidential Information includes, but is not limited to, material nonpublic information. This prohibition applies whether or not the activity constitutes insider trading or securities trading under applicable laws.

While much of this may seem obvious, how insider trading rules apply to prediction markets has been something of a gray area, to put it mildly. And while major prediciton markets explicitly ban the practice in their terms of service, enforcement remains a challenge.

In Apple’s case, the new language explicitly extends restrictions beyond traditional securities trading, making it clear that employees cannot use confidential information to place bets on prediction markets, even when those transactions don’t qualify as insider trading under applicable laws.

You can read Apple’s full 2026 Form 10-K on its Investor Relations page.

#3460. Elden Ring: Malenia, Blade Of Miquella Officially Releases April 2027

The Elden Ring franchise is getting an official new release called Malenia, Blade of Miquella, in April 2027, and fans of the FromSoftware RPG may want to mark their calendars. Even though the legendary studio has not made any announcements for a new game entry in the latest soulslike series, such as the highly rumored sequel to Elden Ring, the franchise is still getting new adjacent releases, more than four years after the original game’s launch. These new arrivals aren’t new titles, but they do celebrate the groundbreaking RPG adored by soulslike fans.

According to a new listing on the official European online Bandai Namco Store, Malenia, Blade of Miquella is set to be released in April 2027. This new release is a miniature from the Figuarts Mini line. The new product, as is implied by its name, is centered around the most iconic boss from Elden Ring, Malenia. The PVC and ABS figure, which is about 10 centimeters in size, is currently available for pre-order for 25,99 € (Euros). This product comes with the Malenia figure, plus an additional swappable arm and a stand.

As such, you can pose Malenia with or without her iconic Hand of Malenia sword, known for executing the deadly Waterfowl Dance attack. The new Malenia release for Elden Ring is part of a much larger collection, which contains figures of several characters from the soulslike RPG. As you can see within the related products on the Malenia, Blade of Miquella page, there are also figures for Melina, Ranni the Witch, Blaidd the Half-Wolf, and even the Raging Wolf.

You can also find the Starscourge Radahn miniature from Elden Ring, though this one is a bit pricier because the iconic demigod comes with his ever-faithful horse, Leonard, as well as two swappable hand parts. This means you can pose Radahn with or without the Starscourge Greatswords, and mounted on or off Leonard. The Starscourge Radahn Figuarts Mini is also available for pre-order, though this product is expected to be released in March 2027, rather than April 2027 like the Malenia, Blade of Miquella Figuarts Mini.

While this figure will hardly provide the same experience you’d get from playing the game, it is a way of remembering and celebrating one of the toughest bosses in Elden Ring. It’s not an easy feat to reach Malenia to start off, as this optional boss is hidden within the center of Miquella’s Haligtree. On top of that, the Goddess of Rot is known for being an exceptionally difficult opponent to deal with. Apart from extremely fast and powerful strikes, she also recovers HP with her attacks, making progress feel lost whenever she lands a hit.

If you’ve defeated her, with or without the help of players like the legendary LetMeSoloHer, having a Malenia figure on your desk can feel like having a trophy of your accomplishment. We’re all waiting for a new entry in the franchise (or any of FromSoftware’s soulslike series, to be honest), but while that does not happen, we can reminisce about some of Elden Ring’s best gameplay moments with this new Malenia figure.

#3458. macOS 27.3 adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look

Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details.

Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and new tools for third-party developers.

Among the smaller changes coming to the Mac is a welcome improvement to Quick Look. As of macOS 27.3 beta 1, .md files are rendered with proper formatting directly in Quick Look, rather than displaying their raw Markdown syntax.

Apple has been expanding Markdown support across its platforms, including the ability to import and export Markdown files in Notes. Markdown has also become increasingly important with the rise of AI agents, which use .md files to store instructions, context, and other information.

In fact, as Federico Viticci noted today on X, Apple’s new Siri AI app skills feature also uses Markdown-based SKILL.md files, allowing developers to provide instructions that help Siri perform complex tasks within their apps.

What a journey for Markdown, @gruber The new Siri AI developer framework now officially uses skills, with specific Markdown guidance for SKILL .md agent files https://t.co/koi8K541le pic.twitter.com/TF72JJZRXc

For the uninitiated, Markdown is a simple text formatting syntax created by John Gruber in 2004, and has since become widely used for writing documentation, publishing content online (including this very post), and, more recently, providing instructions to AI agents.

Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for web writers. Markdown allows you to write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format, then convert it to structurally valid HTML.

In practice, this means you can create headings, bold text, lists, and links using just a few simple characters. And, starting with macOS 27.3, you’ll be able to preview the results directly in Quick Look, without having to open the file in a separate app.

To learn more about Markdown, follow this link.

#3457. The MCU’s Best Line Is Still the Greatest Quote in Franchise History

The MCU is the most successful film franchise in Hollywood history, giving us countless memorable moments — action sequences, quotable scenes, character interactions filled with poignancy and humor, etc. — over the course of its 70+ projects. With such a wealth of options, any argument to be made for one such moment standing as the best in the franchise is likely to be challenged. Oddly enough, being "challenged" just so happens to be the impetus behind the quote that we assert is the greatest in the franchise's history. It's a line that applies to the franchise both on and off the screen, and it's been said more than once by one of the original Avengers, Captain America (Chris Evans), over the course of the franchise's history: "I can do this all day."

The quote is said by Steve Rogers four times over the course of the MCU franchise, with two of those in the film that brought the character into the MCU: Captain America: The First Avenger. The first instance occurs prior to Rogers being given the super serum, where the small and scrawny Rogers is getting beaten up in an alleyway. The attacker is the loud jerk (credited as the "Loud Jerk") Rogers yells at to stop talking during a wartime newsreel shown before a movie. It's no contest: the man is much bigger, and pummels Rogers relentlessly. Only Rogers refuses to stay down, defiantly standing back up and uttering, "I can do this all day."

He can't, or at least shouldn't, but he does, with the words capturing the fighting spirit that refuses to give up, whatever the odds; a spirit that made Rogers the perfect recipient of the serum. So when he says it the next time, during his fight with Red Skull (Hugo Weaving), the quote rings differently. Rogers now has the strength to carry it through, changing the quote from one of admirable defiance to a rallying cry.

The line rings differently, yet again, the third time Rogers says it, during the final one-on-one fight against Iron Man (Robert Downey Jr.) in Captain America: Civil War. Now it's a statement as to how far he'll go to stick to his morals and beliefs, challenging Tony Stark not only physically but ideally, refusing to back down from either. And when we catch up with Rogers after the events of Avengers: Infinity War in Avengers: Endgame, the same drive represented by "I can do this all day" is routed in a different, compassionate way, with Rogers turning his full attention to helping those left behind. And when his 2012 self says the quote later in the film during the fight with his 2023 self, knowing what the quote means makes the moment quite funny, with the two both unwilling to back down.

The strongest challenger for MCU's greatest quote is arguably "I am Iron Man" — the line that, for all intents and purposes, began and ended the MCU's Infinity Saga. Only it applies almost exclusively to the man who said it, Tony Stark, and charts his progression from egotist to self-sacrificing hero, whereas "I can do this all day" goes beyond Steve Rogers to apply to the franchise as a whole. Time and again, the protagonists of the MCU refuse to back down from whoever, or whatever, they're up against. The stand to protect New York from the Chitauri in The Avengers. The final battle against Thanos (Josh Brolin) and his overwhelming army in Avengers: Endgame. Confronting the massive, mighty Galactus (Ralph Ineson), despite the four Fantastics together being smaller than his pinky, in The Fantastic Four: First Steps. And so much more.

Offscreen, the phrase serves as a meta joke of sorts for the MCU, a franchise that has mirrored Captain America's arc, from a scrawny Steve franchise to what it is today. With Avengers: Doomsday set to extend the franchise's dominance at the movie theater, it's easy to picture Kevin Feige saying those exact words. Through the highs of Avengers: Endgame to the lows of Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania, the MCU keeps standing up again, defiant. So long as the fans continue to come out, to see films that deserve to be seen (sorry, Eternals), Feige and company absolutely can, and will, "do this all day."

Flagship phones continue to be the most coveted devices on the market, prized for their top-tier specs, robust software suites, and class-leading cameras. Over the past year, I’ve spent months testing many of the best phones on the market — including the iPhone 18 Pro Max, Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Pixel 11 Pro XL.

Choosing between these heavyweights isn’t as simple as glancing at a spec sheet or trying them out for five minutes at a nearby carrier store. When you plan to shell out well over $1,299, you need to know how each holds up under daily use.

That’s why I’m pitting all three against each other to break down their key strengths, inevitable weaknesses, and most importantly, which flagship is truly worth your money.

6.9-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,868 x 1,320)

6.9-inch Dynamic AMOLED 2X (3,120 x 1,440)

200MP main (f/1.4), 50MP ultrawide (f/1.9), 10MP 3x telephoto (f/2.4), 50MP 5x telephoto (f/2.9)

50MP (f/1.68) main, 48MP (f/1.7) ultrawide, 48MP (f/2.8) 5x telephoto

Black, White, Sky Blue, Cobalt Violet, Silver Shadow, Pink Gold

Even though it’s the one I’ve spent the least amount of time with, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is a marked improvement over the iPhone 17 Pro Max. Apple didn’t hold back here because out of the dozens of devices I’ve tested this year alone, it earns its title as the best camera phone on the market for several reasons.

First and foremost, the main camera features a mechanical variable aperture lens that provides genuine creative control — some examples of which you can see in the gallery above. Wide open, it yields natural optical bokeh, while stopped down, it captures razor-sharp shots edge to edge.

Apple also finally introduced native manual controls courtesy of Pro Controls — a feature notably absent even on the pricier iPhone Duo. This unlocks granular adjustments for shutter speed, aperture, white balance, manual focus, and ISO without forcing you into third-party camera apps. Better yet, these same manual controls extend directly to video recording.

In low light, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is virtually unmatched. While most modern flagships deliver comparable dynamic range under direct midday sun, Apple pulls ahead once the sun dips below the horizon, as you can see in the nighttime sample shots I shot above.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Beyond imaging, the phone is a powerhouse driven by the 2nm A20 Pro chip. Our benchmark testing confirms it sits a level above its rivals in raw computing and graphics processing, yet it remains exceptionally power-efficient — lasting a staggering 18 hours and 27 minutes on our custom battery test to outlast its chief competitors.

Software remains the only mixed bag. While iOS 27 adds welcome Apple Intelligence features — including personal favorites like Reframe — the platform still lags behind the competition in its suite of AI features. Siri AI feels like a breath of fresh air compared to previous generations, but it still falls short of Google’s Gemini. In daily testing, its limited integration with third-party apps keeps it from feeling truly indispensable.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra continues to be the undisputed Swiss Army knife of smartphones, with this year’s model bringing several notable hardware upgrades. It’s also the flagship I’ve spent the most time testing, having pitted it extensively against both its predecessors and its fiercest rivals.

While the S26 Ultra came up just short of the iPhone 18 Pro Max in my camera face-off, it remains vastly superior in one crucial area: telephoto reach. Samsung’s upgraded periscope telephoto lens doesn't just make distance shooting effortless; its combination of optical sharpness and sensor stabilization allowed me to read the minuscule parking regulations on a street sign from clear across the avenue in our sample shots above.

Productivity and software versatility are where the S26 Ultra builds an insurmountable lead. While Samsung’s underlying Google Gemini integration shares parity with other premier Android flagships, it proves just how transformative mobile AI can be when properly integrated. Gemini’s Task Automation genuinely impresses with its ability to execute complex, multi-step actions across disparate apps. Case in point: I was able to place a Dunkin Donuts order through DoorDash with a voice prompt, and it arrived at my door 30 minutes later.

Then there’s the integrated S Pen, an enduring staple you simply won’t find on rival flagships. It remains an unmatched precision tool for annotating documents, sketching concepts, and signing contracts on the go. Even if you don’t pull it out daily, having a built-in active stylus ready without paying extra for an accessory or specialized case adds tremendous value.

Finally, there is the ultimate fallback whenever I accidentally leave my laptop behind: Samsung DeX. Nothing matches the desktop workflow DeX enables when I tether the S26 Ultra to an external monitor or a pair of smart glasses. It transforms the phone into an actual workstation, proving once and for all that I have a full computer sitting in my pocket.

For anyone who prioritizes software above all else, the Pixel 11 Pro XL is the clear contender — and it continues to defend its title as the best AI phone on the market. I’m not just talking about staples like its stock Android 17 interface or Google’s industry-leading pledge of seven years of major OS updates and Pixel Feature Drops.

While it shares baseline Gemini AI features with other Android devices, Google bakes in exclusive software that makes the overall experience feel far more robust. Standouts include Proactive Assistance, which intelligently surfaces contextual actions based on my on-screen activity; Gboard’s Rambler, which offers unmatched conversational voice dictation; and the Creator Studio suite, complete with a built-in teleprompter for mobile video creators. These newcomers sit on top of proven Pixel essentials like Call Screen, Voice Translate, and Pro Res Zoom.

Speaking of zoom, the Pixel 11 Pro XL delivers the longest digital reach in the lineup’s history, maxing out at 120x magnification. When paired with Pro Res Zoom, computational upscaling reconstructs distant details and cleans up grain with remarkable precision — hold it up against the Galaxy S26 Ultra in our sample shots above to see the difference. Creator-focused additions like Magic Capture and custom Camera Looks add even more versatility to an already formidable imaging setup.

The hardware also earns major praise for its 6.8-inch Super Actua display. In our lab testing, it reclaimed the brightness crown, hitting an astonishing 2,877 nits of peak brightness. Direct midday sun simply doesn't wash it out.

The trade-offs, however, stem from familiar hardware limitations. Google's Tensor G6 chip continues to trail Apple and Samsung by noticeable margins across synthetic CPU and GPU benchmarks, which trickles down into less efficient power draw and noticeably shorter battery endurance. Meanwhile, the new rear-mounted HiLight LED feels more like Google’s latest hardware gimmick than a practical tool — reminiscent of the temperature sensor of generations past.

Choosing between the iPhone 18 Pro Max, Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Pixel 11 Pro XL is a much easier call now that all three share the exact same $1,299 starting price. Samsung’s Ultra has traditionally been the most expensive of the bunch, but that’s no longer the case — which makes my final verdict much clearer.

When you’re dropping $1,299 on a smartphone, you shouldn't be forced to compromise on utility. Samsung packs the S26 Ultra with everything I’d want in my pocket to tackle my workday and my daily commute.

#3454. It's Officially The End Of An Era For The Arrowverse

The news that there are not one, but two new Constantine movies reportedly in the works means that Matt Ryan’s underrated Arrowverse take on the Alan More character will soon no longer be the most recent screen version of the iconic antihero. Based on DC's Hellblazer comic book series, 2005’s Constantine starred Keanu Reeves as the eponymous dour demon slayer, an exorcist cursed with the ability to communicate, and fight, with both angels and demons alike.

With slick direction from future I Am Legend director Francis Lawrence and an incredible cast that included Djimon Hounsou, Shia LaBeouf, Tilda Swinton, Peter Stormare, and The Mummy franchise’s Rachel Weisz as the title character’s femme fatale love interest, Constantine was an early R-rated comic book movie that did justice to co-creators Stephen R. Bissette and Alan Moore’s character. However, although Constantine 2 is set to happen eventually, it is not the definitive screen take on the character.

Matt Ryan was cast as John Constantine in 2014’s NBC series Constantine, a dark thriller that took Supernatural’s fun and From Dusk Til Dawn’s edge to make a memorably creepy comic book adaptation. Sadly, Constantine lasted a mere 13 episodes before the series was canceled, but, fortunately, this was not the end of Ryan’s take on the character. In the years that followed, the Arrowverse adopted Ryan’s Constantine, and he appeared in Arrow, Legends of Tomorrow, Batwoman, The Flash, and Harley Quinn.

While Ryan's Constantine also starred in the web series Constantine: City of Demons, it is the iconic DC series Legends of Tomorrow that really warrants further discussion here. Ryan's Constantine was in one episode each other Arrow, Batwoman, The Flash, and Harley Quinn, whereas the actor appeared in a grand total of 47 episodes of Legends of Tomorrow when his recurring season 3 role was fleshed out into a major main role from seasons 4–6.

For those keeping count, that meant that Ryan appeared in almost three times as many Legend of Tomorrow episodes as he did episodes of Constantine itself. The star became one of the highlights of the Arrowverse, while the Arrowverse itself gave Ryan's take on the character of Constantine a whole new lease of life in return. However, after a 12-year reign, Ryan will soon no longer be the most recent live-action version of the character.

Recently, Deadline reported that Evil Dead Wrath's Francis Galluppi is working on a script for another Constantine movie for DC. Seemingly unrelated to the Reeves movie's long-gestating sequel, this movie means that although there could soon be two Constantine live-action movies happening, neither would bring back the Arrowverse’s version of the character.

The fact that HBO made a new version of Watchmen a mere ten years after director Zack Snyder’s take on the iconic graphic novel means Moore is no stranger to seeing his work adapted repeatedly. However, Ryan’s unique trajectory with the character of Constantine, from his swiftly canceled show to joining the Arrowverse, to his long run on Legends of Tomorrow, was a truly chaotic and unpredictable one.

For a long stretch of Legends of Tomorrow, Ryan even ended up playing a different character because DC seemingly had plans for Constantine back then. Of course, these plans never amounted to anything, which meant Ryan could then reprise the role for the DC Animated Movie Universe. However, this also seems to bode badly for the upcoming live-action movie.

From the brevity of Ryan’s show to the long wait for Reeves’ sequel, Constantine seems to be a character that Hollywood has a hard time nailing down. As such, perhaps fans of the Arrowverse need not worry too much after all, as it might still be a while before this proposed Constantine movie actually materializes.

#3453. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: eight to 10 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.
